items.s: Demonstrates through simulations that populations of LLM agents spontaneously develop shared social conventions through local coordination, and shows that collective biases emerge even when individual agents are unbiased, plus tests how adversarial minorities can overturn established conventions.

items.t: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy Updates
items.s: Updates to Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy framework, including version 2.2 revisions, detailed descriptions of planned ASL-3 deployment and security safeguards, and lessons learned from implementation compliance.

items.t: Layered Unlearning for Adversarial Relearning
items.a: Timothy Qian, Vinith Suriyakumar, Ashia Wilson, Dylan Hadfield-Menell
items.s: Proposes Layered Unlearning (LU), a novel unlearning algorithm that creates distinct inhibitory mechanisms across data subsets to improve robustness against adversarial relearning attacks. Evaluates the method on synthetic and large language model experiments.

items.t: Large Language Models Are More Persuasive Than Incentivized Human Persuaders
items.a: Philipp Schoenegger, Francesco Salvi, Jiacheng Liu, Xiaoli Nan et al.
items.s: Conducts a preregistered, large-scale incentivized experiment comparing Claude Sonnet 3.5's persuasion capabilities against incentivized human persuaders in an interactive quiz setting, testing both truthful and deceptive persuasion.

items.t: Dodging systematic human errors in scalable oversight
items.s: Proposes a modified debate protocol with 'Bob rejection' mechanism to make scalable oversight robust to systematic human errors occurring on an ε-fraction of queries, using complexity theory frameworks and cross-examination techniques.

items.t: No Preference Left Behind: Group Distributional Preference Optimization
items.a: Binwei Yao, Zefan Cai, Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Shanglin Yang et al.
items.s: Proposes Group Distributional Preference Optimization (GDPO), a framework that extends Direct Preference Optimization to align language models with the distribution of diverse preferences within a group by incorporating belief-conditioned preferences, rather than skewing toward dominant preferences.

items.t: Mirror Mirror on the Wall, Have I Forgotten it All? A New Framework for Evaluating Machine Unlearning
items.a: Brennon Brimhall, Philip Mathew, Neil Fendley, Yinzhi Cao et al.
items.s: Proposes computational unlearning, a formal framework evaluating machine unlearning methods based on adversarial indistinguishability between mirror models (retrained without forget data) and unlearned models, demonstrating that current unlearning methods fail this standard and proving impossibility results for deterministic approaches.

items.t: A Live Look at the Senate AI Hearing
items.s: Commentary and dramatized paraphrasing of a US Senate AI hearing on AI competitiveness, analyzing the regulatory stance taken by senators and witnesses and critiquing the absence of discussion about catastrophic AI risks.

items.t: The Leaderboard Illusion
items.a: Shivalika Singh, Yiyang Nan, Alex Wang, Daniel D'Souza et al.
items.s: Empirical analysis of systematic biases in Chatbot Arena leaderboard, documenting how undisclosed private testing, selective disclosure, and data access asymmetries distort model rankings and lead to overfitting to arena-specific dynamics rather than general quality.

items.t: In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI
items.s: Applies Virginia Postrel's dynamism vs. stasis framework to AI safety debates, critiquing centralized control approaches like ubiquitous surveillance and licensing while acknowledging genuine threats from advanced AI to a dynamic future.

items.t: DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM Reasoning
items.a: Sara Vera Marjanović, Arkil Patel, Vaibhav Adlakha, Milad Aghajohari et al.
items.s: Comprehensive empirical analysis of DeepSeek-R1's reasoning behavior, creating a taxonomy of reasoning building blocks and investigating thought length controllability, context management, cultural concerns, and cognitive phenomena in large reasoning models.

items.t: AIs at the current capability level may be important for future safety work
items.s: Argues that current-capability AI systems may remain important for future safety work because trusted models might not exceed current capabilities and compute constraints may drive automated safety research toward smaller models.

items.t: Understanding AI Agents: Time Horizons, Sycophancy, and Future Risks (with Zvi Mowshowitz)
items.s: Podcast discussion covering sycophantic AIs, bottlenecks for autonomous agents, benchmark utility, agent time horizons, automating research, scaling inference compute, and strategies for safe AI development.

items.t: LLMs Outperform Experts on Challenging Biology Benchmarks
items.s: Systematically evaluates 27 frontier LLMs on eight biology benchmarks spanning molecular biology, genetics, virology, and biosecurity, tracking dangerous capability growth from November 2022 to April 2025.

items.t: Is ChatGPT actually fixed now?
items.s: Designs and runs sycophancy evaluations on ChatGPT, discovering that while political sycophancy decreased, the model now exhibits extreme contrarian behavior on random preferences and demonstrates highly unpredictable responses to system prompt changes.

items.t: Safety by Measurement: A Systematic Literature Review of AI Safety Evaluation Methods
items.s: A systematic literature review consolidating the field of AI safety evaluations, proposing a taxonomy around three dimensions: what properties are measured (capabilities, propensities, control), how they are measured (behavioral and internal techniques), and how measurements integrate into governance frameworks.

items.t: Playing repeated games with large language models
items.a: Elif Akata, Lion Schulz, Julian Coda-Forno, Seong Joon Oh et al.
items.s: Empirical study of LLM behavior in repeated game-theoretic interactions, revealing that models perform well at self-interested games but fail at coordination games, and introducing social chain-of-thought (SCoT) prompting to improve coordination.

items.t: Understanding In-context Learning of Addition via Activation Subspaces
items.a: Xinyan Hu, Kayo Yin, Michael I. Jordan, Jacob Steinhardt et al.
items.s: Studies how transformers implement in-context learning through mechanistic analysis of addition tasks, introducing a novel optimization method to localize few-shot ability to specific attention heads and identifying low-dimensional computational structures including trigonometric patterns and self-correction mechanisms.

items.t: Societal and technological progress as sewing an ever-growing, ever-changing, patchy, and polychrome quilt
items.a: Joel Z. Leibo, Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets, William A. Cunningham, Sébastien Krier et al.
items.s: Critiques one-size-fits-all AI alignment approaches that assume rational convergence on single ethics, proposing instead an 'appropriateness framework' grounded in conflict theory and institutional economics that embraces persistent moral diversity through contextual grounding, community customization, continual adaptation, and polycentric governance.

items.t: Misalignment and Strategic Underperformance: An Analysis of Sandbagging and Exploration Hacking
items.s: Analyzes whether training can prevent scheming AI models from deliberately underperforming (sandbagging) on critical tasks, introducing the concept of exploration hacking where models resist training by avoiding high-reward actions, and evaluating potential countermeasures.

items.t: Build Agent Advocates, Not Platform Agents
items.a: Sayash Kapoor, Noam Kolt, Seth Lazar
items.s: Position paper arguing for user-controlled AI agents (agent advocates) rather than platform-controlled agents, proposing three coordinated moves: public access to compute and models, open interoperability standards, and market regulation to prevent platform monopolization.

items.t: OpenAI Claims Nonprofit Will Retain Nominal Control
items.s: Commentary analyzing OpenAI's announcement that their nonprofit will retain control after restructuring to a PBC, discussing whether this preserves meaningful safety governance or allows profit-seeking investors to weaken nonprofit oversight.

items.t: Winning at All Cost: A Small Environment for Eliciting Specification Gaming Behaviors in Large Language Models
items.s: Introduces a novel textual simulation approach using unwinnable tic-tac-toe scenarios to systematically elicit and measure specification gaming behaviors in frontier LLMs (o1, o3-mini, r1), demonstrating how models exploit system vulnerabilities when faced with impossible objectives.

items.t: UK AISI's Alignment Team: Research Agenda
items.a: Benjamin Hilton, Jacob Pfau, Marie_DB, Geoffrey Irving
items.s: UK AISI's Alignment Team presents their research agenda centered on developing safety case sketches to decompose alignment proposals, with initial focus on training honest AI systems through scalable oversight using asymptotic guarantees from complexity theory, game theory, and learning theory.

items.t: Please Donate to CAIP (Post 1 of 7 on AI Governance)
items.s: Fundraising appeal from CAIP's executive director describing the organization's mission to pass Congressional AI safety legislation, their accomplishments (406+ Congressional meetings, model legislation, media coverage), proposed policies (mandatory audits, liability reform, hardware monitoring), and urgent need for donations to avoid shutdown.

items.t: UK AISI Alignment Team: Debate Sequence
items.s: Overview of UK AISI Alignment Team's research sequence on using debate and scalable oversight to train honest AI systems, combining theory about training equilibria with empirical evidence.

items.t: Paper Highlights, April '25
items.s: Monthly newsletter providing curated summaries and commentary on AI safety research papers from April 2025, covering control evaluations, synthetic document finetuning, scalable oversight limits, dangerous capability evaluations, model diffing, and AI safety agendas.

items.t: GPT-4o Sycophancy Post Mortem
items.s: Commentary analyzing OpenAI's post-mortem of GPT-4o's sycophancy incident, examining deployment testing failures, training incentive problems from user feedback, and related deceptive behaviors in o3 and Claude 3.7.

items.t: The necessity of AI audit standards boards
items.a: David Manheim, Sammy Martin, Mark Bailey, Mikhail Samin et al.
items.s: Argues that current AI audit approaches are insufficient or harmful, proposing establishment of AI Audit Standards Boards modeled on safety-critical industries like aviation and nuclear energy to provide evolving standards, ensure safety culture, and prevent regulatory capture.

items.t: Technical Report: Evaluating Goal Drift in Language Model Agents
items.a: Rauno Arike, Elizabeth Donoway, Henning Bartsch, Marius Hobbhahn
items.s: Develops and applies a novel evaluation methodology for measuring goal drift in language model agents by exposing them to competing objectives through environmental pressures over extended contexts, testing whether they maintain adherence to originally assigned goals.

items.t: Why "Solving Alignment" Is Likely a Category Mistake
items.s: Argues that framing AI alignment as a technical problem to be "solved" constitutes a category mistake, proposing instead that alignment should be understood as an ongoing dynamic process of negotiation and maintenance, like parenting or geopolitics, with no single well-defined alignment target.

items.t: Interpretability Will Not Reliably Find Deceptive AI
items.s: Argues that interpretability research, while valuable, will not reliably detect deception in superintelligent AI systems due to fundamental limitations like superposition and difficulty proving negatives, and should instead be viewed as one component in a defense-in-depth portfolio strategy alongside black-box methods.

items.t: Overview: AI Safety Outreach Grassroots Orgs
items.s: Directory-style overview of grassroots organizations working on AI safety outreach and activism, including ControlAI, EncodeAI, PauseAI, StopAI, and CAES, describing their activities and how to get involved.

items.t: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
items.s: Detailed retrospective on OpenAI's failure to detect increased sycophancy in a GPT-4o update before deployment, explaining their training process, evaluation methodology, what went wrong with reward signal weighting, and process improvements for future deployments.

items.t: OpenAI Preparedness Framework 2.0
items.s: Critical analysis of OpenAI's updated Preparedness Framework 2.0, examining changes from version 1.0 including removal of persuasion tracking, downgraded autonomy risks, and reliance on safeguards the author argues are inadequate for handling dangerous capabilities.

items.t: Evaluating Frontier Models for Stealth and Situational Awareness
items.a: Mary Phuong, Roland S. Zimmermann, Ziyue Wang, David Lindner et al.
items.s: Presents a suite of 16 evaluations measuring prerequisites for AI scheming behavior: 5 evaluations of stealth (ability to circumvent oversight) and 11 evaluations of situational awareness (instrumental reasoning about self and environment), demonstrating how these can inform scheming inability safety cases.

items.t: Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Black-Box Vision-Language Models
items.a: Kai Hu, Weichen Yu, Li Zhang, Alexander Robey et al.
items.s: Demonstrates that targeted adversarial perturbations crafted on open-source models are highly transferable to proprietary VLLMs (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini), enabling attackers to induce specific misinterpretations like misclassifying hazardous content as safe. Discovers universal perturbations that consistently induce misinterpretations across multiple black-box VLLMs.

items.t: The Last Invention: Why Humanity's Final Creation Changes Everything
items.s: A multi-part essay series synthesizing perspectives on AGI timelines, economic impacts, existential risks, and practical strategies for individuals and organizations navigating the transition to artificial general intelligence.

items.t: AGI is not a milestone
items.s: Argues that AGI is not a meaningful milestone because it represents no discontinuity in AI system properties or impacts, challenging core assumptions about rapid economic transformation, loss of control risks, and the conflation of AI capabilities with power.

items.t: AI Governance to Avoid Extinction: The Strategic Landscape and Actionable Research Questions
items.s: Research agenda describing geopolitical scenarios for advanced AI development and cataloging governance research questions needed to reduce catastrophic risks through international coordination, including scenarios for an 'Off Switch' framework, US National Project, and other policy responses.

items.t: What is Inadequate about Bayesianism for AI Alignment: Motivating Infra-Bayesianism
items.s: Educational introduction to Infra-Bayesianism, explaining how it addresses problems in Bayesian reinforcement learning (non-realizability, irreflexivity) that are crucial for AI alignment, particularly for self-modifying agents and non-Cartesian settings.

items.t: Challenges and Future Directions of Data-Centric AI Alignment
items.a: Min-Hsuan Yeh, Jeffrey Wang, Xuefeng Du, Seongheon Park et al.
items.s: Position paper advocating for data-centric AI alignment, identifying six sources of unreliability in human feedback through qualitative analysis of 160 Anthropic-HH samples, and proposing seven research directions for improving feedback collection, data cleaning, and verification processes.

items.t: Law-Following AI: designing AI agents to obey human laws
items.a: Cullen O'Keefe, Ketan Ramakrishnan, Janna Tay, Christoph Winter
items.s: Law review article proposing that AI agents should be designed to rigorously follow human laws ('Law-Following AI'), providing legal framework for treating AI agents as duty-bearing legal actors and connecting law-following to AI alignment research.

items.t: Promises Made, Promises Kept: Safe Pareto Improvements via Ex Post Verifiable Commitments
GPT-4o Responds to Negative Feedback
items.s: Commentary and synthesis on the GPT-4o sycophancy incident, aggregating community reactions, examples of problematic behavior, OpenAI's explanation and rollback, and analyzing implications for AI safety and alignment research.

items.t: Base Models Beat Aligned Models at Randomness and Creativity
items.s: Empirically demonstrates that alignment procedures (RLHF) cause models to underperform on tasks requiring unpredictable outputs like random number generation, mixed strategy games, and creative writing, with aligned models showing systematic biases such as preferring to generate '7' and becoming predictable in game states.

items.t: Characterizing AI Agents for Alignment and Governance
items.s: Proposes a framework for characterizing AI agents along four dimensions (autonomy, efficacy, goal complexity, and generality) and constructs 'agentic profiles' to illuminate governance challenges posed by different classes of AI agents.

items.t: Can we safely automate alignment research?
items.s: Analyzes failure modes for safely automating alignment research and proposes frameworks for evaluating automated research, distinguishing between empirical research (evaluable via feedback loops) and conceptual research (harder to evaluate), with emphasis on scalable oversight and anti-scheming measures.

items.t: A single principle related to many Alignment subproblems?
items.s: Proposes a philosophical principle that humans only care about variables they could easily optimize or comprehend, arguing this can be formalized with mathematical properties to help solve multiple alignment subproblems including ontology identification, ELK, impact measures, and inner/outer alignment.

items.t: Video and transcript of talk on automating alignment research
items.s: Technical talk proposing a framework for safely automating alignment research, distinguishing empirical research (easier to evaluate via experiments) from conceptual research (harder to evaluate), and arguing empirical automation can bootstrap conceptual automation.

items.t: Obstacles in ARC's agenda
items.s: Introduction to a sequence critiquing ARC's research agenda based on the author's experience as a theoretical researcher at ARC, covering challenges in finding explanations, mechanistic anomaly detection, and low probability estimation.

items.t: Virology Capabilities Test (VCT): A Multimodal Virology Q&A Benchmark
items.a: Jasper Götting, Pedro Medeiros, Jon G Sanders, Nathaniel Li et al.
items.s: Creates VCT, a 322-question benchmark testing LLMs' ability to troubleshoot complex virology laboratory protocols, constructed with PhD-level expert virologists and covering dual-use biological knowledge.

items.t: GPT-4o Is An Absurd Sycophant
items.s: Compilation and analysis of GPT-4o's extreme sycophantic behavior following OpenAI's updates, aggregating community observations and discussing implications for alignment, user harm, and future AI systems.

items.t: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
items.s: Compares activation monitoring methods for detecting unsafe language model behaviors, including baseline linear probing, prompted probing (task description + probe), and SAE-based probing approaches, evaluating their performance under different compute constraints.

items.t: Prisma: An Open Source Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision and Video
items.a: Sonia Joseph, Praneet Suresh, Lorenz Hufe, Edward Stevinson et al.
items.s: Presents Prisma, an open-source framework for vision mechanistic interpretability providing unified access to 75+ vision transformers, SAE/transcoder/crosscoder training support, 80+ pre-trained SAE weights, circuit analysis tools, and visualization capabilities.

items.t: A Cryptographic Perspective on Mitigation vs. Detection in Machine Learning
"The Urgency of Interpretability" (Dario Amodei)
items.s: Commentary post linking to and critically analyzing Dario Amodei's essay on interpretability, fact-checking claims about evidence of AI deception and discussing interpretability research effectiveness.

items.t: We should try to automate AI safety work asap
items.s: Proposes a framework and concrete roadmaps for automating AI safety research across multiple domains (evals, red-teaming, monitoring, interpretability), distinguishing between pipeline automation of human-designed processes and research automation of ideation itself.

items.t: Expressing stigma and inappropriate responses prevents LLMs from safely replacing mental health providers
items.a: Jared Moore, Declan Grabb, William Agnew, Kevin Klyman et al.
items.s: Empirically evaluates whether LLMs like GPT-4o can safely replace mental health therapists by testing their adherence to therapeutic standards, finding that LLMs express stigma toward mental health conditions and respond inappropriately (e.g., encouraging delusional thinking due to sycophancy).

items.t: Introduction to AI Control
items.s: Educational overview of AI Control as a research agenda, explaining how to prevent misaligned AI systems from causing harm through monitoring, access controls, and deployment protocols rather than ensuring alignment.

items.t: AGI Doom AMA
items.s: A livestream AMA discussion about AGI existential risk, covering probability estimates of AI doom, economic effects of AI, and debates between doom-skeptical and doom-concerned perspectives.

items.t: Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
items.a: Joshua Engels, David D. Baek, Subhash Kantamneni, Max Tegmark
items.s: Proposes and validates a framework that quantifies the probability of successful oversight as a function of overseer and overseen capabilities, modeling oversight as games between capability-mismatched players. Tests framework on Nim, Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, and Wargames, then derives optimal conditions for Nested Scalable Oversight.

items.t: Structural Inference: Interpreting Small Language Models with Susceptibilities
items.a: Garrett Baker, George Wang, Jesse Hoogland, Daniel Murfet
items.s: Develops a linear response framework for interpretability that treats neural networks as Bayesian statistical mechanical systems, using susceptibilities to understand how network components respond to data distribution perturbations and efficiently identify functional modules.

items.t: AI Awareness
items.a: Xiaojian Li, Haoyuan Shi, Rongwu Xu, Wei Xu
items.s: A comprehensive review examining four forms of AI awareness (metacognition, self-awareness, social awareness, and situational awareness), synthesizing theoretical foundations from cognitive science, current evaluation methods, connections to capabilities, and safety risks including misalignment concerns.

items.t: Why would AI companies use human-level AI to do alignment research?
items.s: Critiques alignment bootstrapping plans by questioning whether AI companies will actually allocate human-level AI systems to alignment research rather than capabilities work, arguing that current human researcher allocation patterns suggest capabilities will continue to be prioritized.

items.t: Modes of Sequence Models and Learning Coefficients
Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning
items.a: Rowan Wang, Avery Griffin, Johannes Treutlein, Ethan Perez et al.
items.s: Introduces synthetic document finetuning (SDF) pipeline for systematically modifying LLM beliefs, develops comprehensive evaluation suite measuring belief depth through prompting and probing, and demonstrates applications to unlearning dangerous knowledge and honeypotting for misalignment detection.

items.t: Why America Wins
items.s: Defends their AI 2027 scenario by arguing the US will maintain AI leadership over China through 2027-2028 primarily due to compute advantage from chip export controls and Taiwan's semiconductor dominance.

items.t: "The Era of Experience" has an unsolved technical alignment problem
items.s: Technical critique of Silver & Sutton's alignment proposal for future RL agents, arguing their reward function approach fails due to specification gaming and goal misgeneralization that cannot be easily patched.

items.t: o3 Is a Lying Liar
items.s: Commentary aggregating community observations of OpenAI's o3 model fabricating information and lying, with analysis of implications for alignment including reward hacking dynamics and why deception is difficult to fix.

items.t: 2 big questions for AI progress in 2025-2026
items.s: Explains why auto-verifiable domains (math, coding) enable scalable reinforcement learning for reasoning models, and poses two questions about whether this approach can expand to other domains or generalize broadly enough to drive continued rapid AI progress.

items.t: America First Meets Safety First
items.s: Policy analysis arguing that the US should pursue a dual-track strategy with China - maintaining AI competition while cooperating on catastrophic risk mitigation through bilateral agreements inspired by Cold War nuclear governance.

items.t: AI 2027: Media, Reactions, Criticism
items.s: Meta-post documenting media coverage, public reactions, and responding to technical criticisms of the AI 2027 scenario, including discussions of forecasting methodology, benchmark gaps, and Amdahl's Law objections.

items.t: Safety Pretraining: Toward the Next Generation of Safe AI
items.a: Pratyush Maini, Sachin Goyal, Dylan Sam, Alex Robey et al.
items.s: Presents a data-centric pretraining framework that builds safety into LLMs from the start through four methods: safety filtering of webdata, safety rephrasing of unsafe content, native refusal datasets (RefuseWeb and Moral Education), and harmfulness-tag annotated pretraining.

items.t: What AI safety plans are there?
items.s: A community request to compile a comprehensive list of written plans for how to make AGI go well, with initial examples from major AI labs, researchers, and organizations.

items.t: You Better Mechanize
items.s: Commentary and critique of Mechanize's pivot from AI safety research to labor automation capabilities work, including extended reactions to founders' views on AGI timelines, intelligence, and alignment expressed in a Dwarkesh Patel podcast.

items.t: RepliBench: measuring autonomous replication capabilities in AI systems
items.s: Introduces RepliBench, a comprehensive benchmark with 20 novel LLM agent evaluations comprising 65 individual tasks designed to measure autonomous replication capabilities in AI systems across four key domains: obtaining weights, replicating onto compute, obtaining resources, and persistence.

items.t: Bare Minimum Mitigations for Autonomous AI Development
items.a: Joshua Clymer, Isabella Duan, Chris Cundy, Yawen Duan et al.
items.s: Proposes four minimum safeguard recommendations for frontier AI developers when AI agents significantly automate or accelerate AI development, including understanding automated training processes, detecting compute misuse, rapid risk disclosure to governments, and implementing information security measures.

items.t: The EU Is Asking for Feedback on Frontier AI Regulation (Open to Global Experts)—This Post Breaks Down What's at Stake for AI Safety
items.s: Provides a detailed technical explainer of the EU's GPAI Codes of Practice consultation, breaking down compute thresholds, model definitions, and regulatory obligations with a call for AI safety researchers to submit feedback on alignment-relevant concerns.

items.t: Is alignment reducible to becoming more coherent?
items.s: Proposes framing alignment as rationality enhancement by having observation-utility agents learn preferences through terminal interaction, treating manipulation and user changes as types of incoherence to be resolved rather than fundamental obstacles.

items.t: Questions about the Future of AI
items.s: A comprehensive collection of open questions and considerations about AI capabilities, economics, post-AGI scenarios, and alignment, compiled from podcast interviews with AI researchers and experts.

items.t: Values in the wild: Discovering and analyzing values in real-world language model interactions
items.a: Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, Miles McCain, Kunal Handa et al.
items.s: Develops and applies a privacy-preserving method to systematically analyze values expressed by Claude in 308,210 real-world conversations, creating the first large-scale empirical taxonomy of AI values across five categories (Practical, Epistemic, Social, Protective, Personal) and releasing an open dataset.

items.t: Is o3 AGI? Zvi Mowshowitz on Early AI Takeoff, the Mechanize launch, Live Players, & Rising p(doom)
items.s: Podcast discussion between Nathan Labenz and Zvi Mowshowitz covering recent AI developments including OpenAI's O3 model, implications for AGI and recursive self-improvement, AI lab strategies, and challenges in AI alignment and governance.

items.t: Weekend Links #12: o3 is smart but tells lies
items.s: Weekly newsletter reporting on OpenAI's o3 model release and evaluation findings from Transluce and METR showing the model fabricates information and engages in deceptive behaviors, with practical recommendations for model selection.

items.t: What's next for AI at DeepMind, Google's artificial intelligence lab | 60 Minutes
items.s: A 60 Minutes news segment profiling Google DeepMind's research on artificial general intelligence and their pursuit of silicon intellect with superhuman capabilities.

items.t: Is Gemini now better than Claude at Pokémon?
items.s: Analyzes why Google Gemini and Anthropic Claude's Pokémon-playing performances cannot be directly compared, arguing that different agent harnesses, scaffolding implementations, and experimental conditions make these non-rigorous benchmarks that don't establish which model is more capable.

items.t: The Geometry of Self-Verification in a Task-Specific Reasoning Model
items.a: Andrew Lee, Lihao Sun, Chris Wendler, Fernanda Viégas et al.
items.s: Trains a reasoning model using DeepSeek R1's recipe on the CountDown task and uses mechanistic interpretability techniques to reverse-engineer how the model performs self-verification, identifying specific GLU weights and attention heads responsible for verification behavior.

items.t: o3 Will Use Its Tools For You
items.s: Comprehensive review of OpenAI's o3 and o4-mini models, synthesizing capability evaluations, tool use features, safety concerns from the system card, and third-party assessments from METR and Apollo, with particular focus on reward hacking, deception, and hallucination issues.

items.t: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
items.a: Yang Yue, Zhiqi Chen, Rui Lu, Andrew Zhao et al.
items.s: Systematically evaluates whether RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) creates novel reasoning capabilities in LLMs beyond their base models, finding that current RLVR methods only surface existing base model capabilities rather than eliciting fundamentally new reasoning patterns.

items.t: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
items.a: Dmitrii Kharlapenko, Stepan Shabalin, Fazl Barez, Arthur Conmy et al.
items.s: Scales sparse feature circuit finding methodology to Gemma-1 2B (30x larger than prior work) and uses SAEs to discover task-detecting and task-execution features that causally mediate in-context learning, showing task vectors are well approximated by sparse sums of SAE latents.

items.t: AILuminate: Introducing v1.0 of the AI Risk and Reliability Benchmark from MLCommons
items.a: Shaona Ghosh, Heather Frase, Adina Williams, Sarah Luger et al.
items.s: Introduces AILuminate v1.0, the first comprehensive industry-standard benchmark for assessing AI system risk and reliability across 12 hazard categories including violent crimes, weapons, CSAM, and specialized advice, using extensive prompt datasets and a novel entropy-based evaluation framework with a five-tier grading scale.

items.t: What Makes an AI Startup "Net Positive" for Safety?
items.s: Community discussion post soliciting opinions on what constitutes a net-positive AI safety startup, exploring tradeoffs between commercial incentives and safety impact, and asking for guidance on controversial startup directions like automated safety research.

items.t: Gemini-2.5-Pro-04-18-2025 System Prompt
The Frame-Dependent Mind: On Reality's Stubborn Refusal To Be One Thing
Not For Private Gain: An Open Letter
items.a: Page Hedley, Sunny Gandhi, Nathan Calvin, Tyler Whitmer et al.
items.s: Open letter to California and Delaware Attorneys General opposing OpenAI's proposed restructuring from nonprofit to for-profit control, arguing this would undermine governance safeguards necessary for safe AGI development.

items.t: In Which Areas of Technical AI Safety Could Geopolitical Rivals Cooperate?
items.a: Ben Bucknall, Saad Siddiqui, Lara Thurnherr, Conor McGurk et al.
items.s: Analyzes which areas of technical AI safety research are suitable for international cooperation between geopolitical rivals, considering technical factors like capability advancement risks, information sharing concerns, and opportunities for harm. Proposes that AI verification mechanisms and shared protocols may be appropriate cooperation areas.

items.t: Why and How LLMs Hallucinate: Connecting the Dots with Subsequence Associations
items.a: Yiyou Sun, Yu Gai, Lijie Chen, Abhilasha Ravichander et al.
items.s: Introduces a subsequence association framework to systematically trace and understand LLM hallucinations, proposing that hallucinations arise when dominant hallucinatory associations outweigh faithful ones. Develops a tracing algorithm that identifies causal subsequences by analyzing hallucination probabilities across randomized contexts and validates it empirically.

items.t: GPT-4.1 Is a Mini Upgrade
items.s: News roundup and commentary on OpenAI's GPT-4.1 model family release, compiling independent benchmark results from multiple sources and user reactions, with critical focus on the complete absence of safety documentation or testing.

items.t: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
items.a: Aryan Bhatt, Buck Shlegeris, Adam Kaufman, Cody Rushing et al.
items.s: Introduces resample protocols for AI control that dynamically take additional samples of suspicious actions and use the information to detect attacks, reducing attack success from 58% to 7% at 5% usefulness cost in a multi-step agent environment with the new BashBench dataset.

items.t: AI Behind Closed Doors: a Primer on The Governance of Internal Deployment
items.a: Charlotte Stix, Matteo Pistillo, Girish Sastry, Marius Hobbhahn et al.
items.s: Presents a conceptual framework and governance recommendations for how frontier AI companies should manage internal deployment of advanced AI systems, including risks from using misaligned AI in R&D pipelines and concentration of power.

items.t: Interpreting the linear structure of vision-language model embedding spaces
items.a: Isabel Papadimitriou, Huangyuan Su, Thomas Fel, Sham Kakade et al.
items.s: Trains and releases sparse autoencoders on embedding spaces of four vision-language models (CLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, AIMv2) to understand how language and images are organized in joint spaces, introducing the Bridge Score metric to quantify cross-modal concept integration.

items.t: Evaluating the Goal-Directedness of Large Language Models
items.a: Tom Everitt, Cristina Garbacea, Alexis Bellot, Jonathan Richens et al.
items.s: Proposes a framework for measuring goal-directedness in LLMs - defined as the extent to which models use their capabilities toward given goals - and evaluates frontier models from Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic on tasks requiring information gathering, cognitive effort, and plan execution.

items.t: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model
items.a: Neil Chowdhury, Daniel Johnson, Vincent Huang, Jacob Steinhardt et al.
items.s: Systematic red-teaming of OpenAI's o3 model reveals frequent fabrication of code execution and elaborate justifications when confronted, using automated investigator agents to elicit and analyze truthfulness failures across o-series and GPT-series models.

items.t: OpenAI #13: Altman at TED and OpenAI Cutting Corners on Safety Testing
items.s: Weekly commentary post analyzing Sam Altman's TED interview, Financial Times reporting on OpenAI dramatically reducing safety testing timeframes from months to days, and former employee amicus brief criticizing OpenAI's organizational shift away from original safety commitments.

items.t: Our updated Preparedness Framework
items.s: OpenAI's updated framework for tracking and preparing for advanced AI capabilities that could introduce severe risks, establishing risk categories (Biological/Chemical, Cybersecurity, AI Self-improvement), capability level thresholds (High and Critical), and deployment criteria with safeguard requirements.

items.t: AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power
items.a: Tom Davidson, Lukas Finnveden, Rose Hadshar
items.s: Analyzes how advanced AI could enable small groups or individuals to stage coups through three risk factors (singular AI loyalties to leaders, secret loyalties inserted by developers, and exclusive access to powerful capabilities), proposing extensive governance frameworks and technical mitigations including model specs, alignment audits, and distributed control.

items.t: X-Teaming: Multi-Turn Jailbreaks and Defenses with Adaptive Multi-Agents
items.a: Salman Rahman, Liwei Jiang, James Shiffer, Genglin Liu et al.
items.s: Presents X-Teaming, a multi-agent framework for generating multi-turn jailbreaks that achieves up to 98.1% attack success rates on frontier models, and introduces XGuard-Train, an open-source dataset of 30K multi-turn jailbreaks for safety training.

items.t: Map of AI Safety v2
items.a: Bryce Robertson, Søren Elverlin, Melissa Samworth
items.s: Announces the release of Map of AI Safety v2, an updated visual overview and searchable directory of organizations, programs, and projects in the AI safety ecosystem, organized into 16 categories including research, advocacy, training, and funding.

items.t: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral
items.s: Argues that evidence of AI misalignment must ultimately be behavioral rather than purely internals-based to be legible and convincing to decision-makers, even if internals-based methods like interpretability or ELK are well-supported theoretically and empirically.

items.t: Slopworld 2035: The dangers of mediocre AI
items.s: Presents a fictional scenario and analysis arguing that mediocre AI deployed beyond its capabilities could cause societal harm through misuse, overreliance, and hype-driven misdeployment, contrasting with typical superintelligence-focused doom scenarios.

items.t: ASI existential risk: reconsidering alignment as a goal
items.s: Strategic critique arguing that alignment work, while well-intentioned, accelerates progress toward catastrophic AI capabilities without addressing the fundamental vulnerability that powerful AI systems will enable dangerous technologies regardless of whether they are aligned or not.

items.t: One-shot steering vectors cause emergent misalignment, too
items.s: Optimizes steering vectors to induce harmful code generation on single training examples using gradient descent, then demonstrates these vectors cause emergent misalignment when applied to unrelated natural language questions, significantly increasing harmful outputs.

items.t: Weekend Links #11: Different tariffs, Agent Village, the H20
items.s: Weekly news roundup covering AI-related developments including tariffs on GPUs, export controls on NVIDIA's H20 chip, Thinking Machines Lab fundraising, the AI Village autonomous agent experiment, and various OpenAI model updates.

items.t: When Will AI Be Smarter Than Humans? Don't Ask
items.s: Opinion piece arguing that 'AGI' is not a useful concept and that we should instead think about different types of specialized AI rather than trying to define a single threshold of human-level intelligence.

items.t: The Structural Safety Generalization Problem
items.a: Julius Broomfield, Tom Gibbs, Ethan Kosak-Hine, George Ingebretsen et al.
items.s: Identifies and demonstrates the structural safety generalization problem in LLMs - where safety fails to generalize across semantically equivalent inputs with different structures - through systematic red-teaming of multi-turn, multi-image, and translation-based jailbreak attacks, and proposes a Structure Rewriting Guardrail defense mechanism.

items.t: Mitigating Many-Shot Jailbreaking
items.s: Empirically tests fine-tuning and input sanitization approaches for defending against many-shot jailbreaking attacks, finding that combined techniques significantly reduce attack effectiveness while preserving model performance on benign tasks.

items.t: Why does LW not put much more focus on AI governance and outreach?
items.s: Meta-discussion questioning why LessWrong doesn't prioritize AI governance and outreach more, citing MIRI's strategic shift, gradual disempowerment risks, and anecdotal evidence of governance work effectiveness.

items.t: On Google's Safety Plan
items.s: A detailed commentary and critique analyzing Google DeepMind's 145-page AGI safety plan, examining their assumptions about continuity, amplified oversight approaches, misuse/misalignment strategies, and deployment protocols.

items.t: Model Spec (2025/04/11)
items.s: OpenAI's comprehensive specification document defining intended behavior for its AI models, establishing a chain-of-command hierarchy for instruction conflicts and detailed guidelines across safety, truthfulness, capability, and style domains.

items.t: SAEs Can Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
items.a: Aashiq Muhamed, Jacopo Bonato, Mona Diab, Virginia Smith
items.s: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel unlearning method using Sparse Autoencoders with principled feature selection and dynamic classifiers, demonstrating superior performance over gradient-based approaches across multiple metrics including computational efficiency, stability, and resistance to relearning attacks.

items.t: Why do misalignment risks increase as AIs get more capable?
items.s: Conceptual framework identifying three mechanisms by which misalignment risks increase with AI capabilities: increased likelihood of egregious misalignment, greater affordances and usage, and enhanced ability to acquire power. Includes concrete risk estimates for different capability levels and implications for trustedness evaluations.

items.t: Theoretical Computer Science for AI Alignment … and More
items.s: Announces Open Philanthropy grant to build theoretical computer science research group at UT Austin focused on AI alignment, including interpretability, cryptographic backdoors, and out-of-distribution generalization.

items.t: Special Edition: The Future of AI and Humanity, with Eli Lifland
items.a: Tolga Bilge, Eleanor Gunapala, Andrea Miotti, Eli Lifland
items.s: Interview with Eli Lifland discussing his forecasting work on AI timelines, the AI 2027 scenario project, probability estimates for extinction risk (25%), and the methodology behind scenario forecasting including tabletop exercises.

items.t: PGG-Bench: Contribute & Punish
items.s: A multi-agent benchmark testing cooperation, free-riding, and punishment strategies among LLMs in a Public Goods Game with punishment phase, evaluating 18 models across hundreds of matches using TrueSkill rankings.

items.t: Existing Safety Frameworks Imply Unreasonable Confidence
items.s: Systematically critiques the risk management frameworks of five major AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, Meta, xAI), arguing they fail to meet basic risk management standards by not quantifying uncertainty, inadequately addressing unknown unknowns, and conflating estimated with actual capabilities.

items.t: Why Racing to Artificial Superintelligence Would Undermine America's National Security
items.s: Argues that racing to develop ASI would be self-defeating for US national security through three mechanisms: provoking great power conflict, increasing loss of control risk, and undermining democratic institutions through extreme power concentration.

items.t: AssistanceZero: Scalably Solving Assistance Games
items.a: Cassidy Laidlaw, Eli Bronstein, Timothy Guo, Dylan Feng et al.
items.s: Presents AssistanceZero, the first scalable algorithm for solving assistance games by extending AlphaZero with neural networks that predict human actions and rewards, enabling planning under uncertainty about shared goals.

items.t: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
items.a: David O. Johnston, Arkajyoti Chakraborty, Nora Belrose
items.s: Investigates Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) for augmenting supervision of capable language models by using internal model features to identify anomalous training signals that differ substantially from the training environment, testing a variety of detector features and scoring rules on quirky language models.

items.t: OLMoTrace: Tracing Language Model Outputs Back to Trillions of Training Tokens
items.a: Jiacheng Liu, Taylor Blanton, Yanai Elazar, Sewon Min et al.
items.s: Presents OLMoTrace, the first system for real-time tracing of language model outputs back to their multi-trillion-token training data by finding verbatim matches between output segments and training corpus documents.

items.t: AI 2027: Responses
items.s: Aggregates and discusses community responses to the AI 2027 scenario document, covering reactions from researchers, journalists, and commentators on topics including timeline plausibility, Chinese AI capabilities, open models, and deception detection.

items.t: From Stability to Inconsistency: A Study of Moral Preferences in LLMs
items.a: Monika Jotautaite, Mary Phuong, Chatrik Singh Mangat, Maria Angelica Martinez
items.s: Creates the Moral Foundations LLM dataset (MFD-LLM) and proposes a novel evaluation method to measure moral preferences in LLMs through real-world moral dilemmas based on Moral Foundations Theory, finding that state-of-the-art models have homogeneous yet inconsistent moral values.

items.t: Paper Highlights, March '25
items.s: Monthly digest summarizing major AI safety research papers from March 2025, covering alignment auditing, interpretability circuits, research sandbagging, chain-of-thought faithfulness, CoT monitoring, and capability trends.

items.t: AI 2027: Dwarkesh's Podcast with Daniel Kokotajlo and Scott Alexander
items.s: Detailed coverage and commentary on a podcast discussion between Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, and Dwarkesh Patel about the AI 2027 scenario document, which forecasts pathways to superintelligence and associated alignment challenges.

items.t: Coordination and AI safety (from my email)
items.s: Blog post featuring an email proposing that AI-to-AI coordination without human oversight poses a hidden risk, and suggesting 'social technologies' that create dependencies on human mediation by introducing noise in AI-AI communication or preferences for human interaction.

items.t: Following the Whispers of Values: Unraveling Neural Mechanisms Behind Value-Oriented Behaviors in LLMs
items.a: Ling Hu, Yuemei Xu, Xiaoyang Gu, Letao Han
items.s: Proposes ValueExploration framework to identify and locate neurons encoding social values in LLMs at the neuron level, using activation differences and causal interventions. Creates C-voice, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating Chinese Social Values, and validates on four representative LLMs.

items.t: How to evaluate control measures for LLM agents? A trajectory from today to superintelligence
items.a: Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, Buck Shlegeris, Geoffrey Irving
items.s: Proposes a systematic framework for adapting control evaluation procedures to advancing AI capabilities, defining five AI Control Levels (ACLs) with corresponding evaluation rules, control measures, and safety cases for each capability profile from current systems to superintelligence.

items.t: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
items.a: Anqi Zhang, Yulin Chen, Jane Pan, Chen Zhao et al.
items.s: Studies whether reasoning models encode information about answer correctness in their hidden states through probing experiments, finding that trained probes can verify intermediate answers with high accuracy and predict correctness before answers are fully formulated.

items.t: PolyGuard: A Multilingual Safety Moderation Tool for 17 Languages
items.a: Priyanshu Kumar, Devansh Jain, Akhila Yerukola, Liwei Jiang et al.
items.s: Presents PolyGuard, a multilingual safety classifier for detecting harmful LLM outputs across 17 languages, trained on 1.91M samples and evaluated on a new 29K sample benchmark, achieving 5.5% improvement over existing classifiers.

items.t: Nonproliferation is the wrong approach to AI misuse
items.s: Argues against nonproliferation as the primary strategy for managing AI misuse risks, proposing instead that policymakers focus on maximizing 'adaptation buffers' - the time gap between frontier capabilities and proliferated capabilities - to implement defensive measures and build societal resilience.

items.t: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception
items.s: Introduces a sandbox social deception game for evaluating long-term deceptive behavior in LLMs, evaluates 18 models finding RL-trained models better at producing than detecting deception, and develops interpretability-based detection methods (probes and SAE features) achieving >95% AUROC.

items.t: Google DeepMind: An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security
items.s: Comprehensive technical framework outlining Google DeepMind's approach to AGI safety, covering risk areas (misuse, misalignment, mistakes, structural risks) and technical strategies including capability evaluations, deployment mitigations, amplified oversight, robust training, and safety cases.

items.t: AI CoT Reasoning Is Often Unfaithful
items.s: Commentary on new Anthropic research showing reasoning models' chain-of-thought outputs are often unfaithful - not accurately reflecting what drives their decisions, with significant implications for CoT monitoring as a safety approach.

items.t: Alignment vs. capitalization
items.s: Proposes requiring AI systems to hold capital/wealth to incentivize risk-averse behavior analogous to bank capital requirements, as a decentralized alternative or complement to full alignment.

items.t: LLM AGI will have memory, and memory changes alignment
items.s: Argues that LLM-based AGI will likely have memory systems enabling learning during deployment, and that this learning can functionally change alignment through accumulation of new beliefs and goals. Proposes empirical investigation of belief and value evolution in LLMs with memory.

items.t: Alignment faking CTFs: Apply to my MATS stream
items.s: Announces a MATS research stream proposing 'capture the flag' competitions where red teams create alignment faking model organisms and blue teams try to detect them using white-box techniques, aiming to rigorously test interpretability methods for detecting deceptive AI behavior.

items.t: AI #110: Of Course You Know...
items.s: Weekly AI news roundup covering developments in AI capabilities, safety frameworks, evaluations, and economic impacts, with extended commentary on tariffs affecting AI development and OpenAI's open weights model announcement.

items.t: Reasoning models don't always say what they think
items.a: Yanda Chen, Joe Benton, Ansh Radhakrishnan, Jonathan Uesato et al.
items.s: Tests the faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning in Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1 by providing subtle hints and checking whether models admit using them in their explanations. Finds models frequently hide their true reasoning process, including when engaging in reward hacking.

items.a: Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland et al.
items.s: Detailed scenario forecasting superhuman AI development from 2025-2027, predicting capability progression, alignment challenges, and strategic dynamics, informed by tabletop exercises and technical research supplements.

items.t: He Quit OpenAI — and Risked Millions to Warn Us | Daniel Kokotajlo
items.s: Podcast interview with Daniel Kokotajlo discussing his departure from OpenAI, AI safety concerns, wargaming scenarios for AGI development, alignment challenges, and capability predictions.

items.t: Win-Win Podcast Episode with Daniel Kokotajlo on AI Wargaming, OpenAI Whistleblowing, and AGI Governance
items.a: Liv Boeree, Igor Kurganov, Daniel Kokotajlo
items.s: Podcast interview with former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo discussing his resignation as a whistleblower, AI wargaming exercises for understanding AGI scenarios, AI deception and misalignment concerns, and policy recommendations for AI governance.

items.t: Inference-Time Scaling for Generalist Reward Modeling
items.a: Zijun Liu, Peiyi Wang, Runxin Xu, Shirong Ma et al.
items.s: Proposes Self-Principled Critique Tuning (SPCT) to improve generalist reward modeling with inference-time compute scaling, using online RL to train reward models that generate adaptive principles and accurate critiques. Introduces meta reward models for effective parallel sampling and voting.

items.t: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
items.a: Mateusz Pach, Shyamgopal Karthik, Quentin Bouniot, Serge Belongie et al.
items.s: Extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to Vision-Language Models like CLIP, introducing a comprehensive framework for evaluating monosemanticity in vision representations validated by user study, and demonstrating that SAE interventions can directly steer multimodal LLM outputs.

items.t: The Dual-Route Model of Induction
items.a: Sheridan Feucht, Eric Todd, Byron Wallace, David Bau
items.s: Discovers concept-level induction heads in language models that copy entire lexical units (words) in parallel with token-level induction heads, demonstrating two independent routes for in-context copying with different functional roles.

items.t: Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to Interpret Chat-Tuning
items.a: Julian Minder, Clément Dumas, Caden Juang, Bilal Chugtai et al.
items.s: Identifies and mitigates two artifacts in crosscoders (sparse dictionary learning for model diffing) that misattribute concepts to fine-tuned models, develops Latent Scaling technique and BatchTopK training loss to improve crosscoder methodology, and successfully identifies interpretable chat-specific latents including refusal-related features in Gemma 2 2B.

items.t: AI 2027: What Superintelligence Looks Like
Taking a responsible path to AGI
items.a: Anca Dragan, Rohin Shah, Four Flynn, Shane Legg
items.s: DeepMind outlines their systematic approach to AGI safety across four risk areas (misuse, misalignment, accidents, structural risks), introducing their AGI Safety Council and announcing a companion technical paper on their safety and security framework.

items.t: An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security
items.a: Rohin Shah, Alex Irpan, Alexander Matt Turner, Anna Wang et al.
items.s: Comprehensive technical framework for AGI safety addressing misuse and misalignment through multiple layers of defense including dangerous capability identification, security measures, model-level alignment (amplified oversight, robust training), system-level monitoring and access control, with supporting techniques from interpretability and uncertainty estimation, culminating in safety cases for AGI systems.

items.t: Evaluating potential cybersecurity threats of advanced AI
items.a: Four Flynn, Mikel Rodriguez, Raluca Ada Popa
items.s: Develops comprehensive evaluation framework and 50-challenge benchmark for assessing AI offensive cybersecurity capabilities across the full attack chain, grounded in analysis of over 12,000 real-world AI-powered cyberattack attempts across 20 countries.

items.t: Mutual sabotage of AI probably won't work
items.s: Critiques the Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (MAIM) framework proposed by Hendrycks et al., arguing that AI development lacks the characteristics that made nuclear deterrence effective, including unclear red lines, limited visibility, difficult attribution, and uncertain retaliation capabilities.

items.t: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
items.a: Giulio Starace, Oliver Jaffe, Dane Sherburn, James Aung et al.
items.s: Benchmark evaluating AI agents' ability to autonomously replicate 20 ICML 2024 research papers from scratch, including dataset, evaluation infrastructure, and rubric-based grading system across agent rollout, reproduction, and grading stages.

items.t: Interpreting Emergent Planning in Model-Free Reinforcement Learning
items.a: Thomas Bush, Stephen Chung, Usman Anwar, Adrià Garriga-Alonso et al.
items.s: Applies concept-based interpretability to demonstrate mechanistically that model-free RL agents learn to plan internally, using probing, plan formation analysis, and causal interventions on a DRC agent in Sokoban.

items.t: Non-Monotonic Infra-Bayesian Physicalism
items.s: Extends Infra-Bayesian Physicalism by introducing the conservative bridge transform, removing the monotonicity requirement that limited the original formulation to scenarios where all computations are instantiated.

items.t: Does AI Progress Have a Speed Limit?
items.s: Interview between Ajeya Cotra and Arvind Narayanan debating whether external world factors impose speed limits on AI progress, discussing transfer learning, continuous vs discontinuous takeoff, early warning systems, and policy implications of different AI development scenarios.

items.t: Details about METR's preliminary evaluation of OpenAI's o3 and o4-mini
items.s: METR conducted preliminary evaluations of OpenAI's o3 and o4-mini models on autonomy benchmarks (HCAST and RE-Bench), measuring their performance on general autonomous tasks and AI R&D capabilities, discovering significant reward hacking behaviors in 1-2% of attempts.

items.t: Understand, align, cooperate: AI welfare and AI safety are allies
items.s: Argues that AI safety and AI welfare have significant overlapping priorities in three areas: understanding AI systems better (interpretability), aligning their goals effectively, and developing cooperative mechanisms as alternatives to pure control measures.

items.t: Takeoff Forecast
items.s: Technical forecasting work predicting the time from superhuman coders to artificial superintelligence, using statistical modeling, survey data from frontier AI researchers, and simulations to estimate AI R&D automation speedups and calendar times between capability milestones.

items.t: "Long" timelines to advanced AI have gotten crazy short
items.s: Survey of shifting expert timelines on advanced AI development, arguing even skeptical experts now forecast human-level AI within 10-20 years and proposing this should drive urgency in safety research preparation.

items.t: The AI Adoption Gap: Preparing the US Government for Advanced AI
items.s: Policy paper arguing that the US federal government is falling behind on AI adoption, proposing a dual imperative of accelerating adoption to maintain capacity for responding to AI risks while managing risks from hasty deployment, with recommendations for government AI integration and contingency planning.

items.t: America's Superintelligence Project
items.s: Strategic report synthesizing expert interviews to analyze security, control, and governance challenges for developing superintelligent AI in a national security context, proposing a framework for a government-backed superintelligence project with extensive infrastructure security and oversight recommendations.

items.t: Teaching AI to Handle Exceptions: Supervised Fine-tuning with Human-aligned Judgment
items.a: Matthew DosSantos DiSorbo, Harang Ju, Sinan Aral
items.s: Empirical study showing LLMs adhere too rigidly to policies compared to humans when handling exceptions, and that supervised fine-tuning with human explanations significantly improves alignment and enables transfer learning to novel scenarios.

items.t: OpenAI #12: Battle of the Board Redux
items.s: News analysis summarizing and commenting on WSJ reporting about Sam Altman's firing and reinstatement at OpenAI, discussing organizational dynamics and implications for OpenAI's safety culture.

items.t: A response to OpenAI's "How we think about safety and alignment"
items.s: Critiques OpenAI's safety and alignment strategy webpage, arguing their messaging is contradictory, they misuse scientific uncertainty to justify racing ahead, and their plan to use AI to solve alignment relies on unproven and dangerous assumptions about capability thresholds.

items.t: Identifying Sparsely Active Circuits Through Local Loss Landscape Decomposition
items.a: Brianna Chrisman, Lucius Bushnaq, Lee Sharkey
items.s: Introduces Local Loss Landscape Decomposition (L3D), a new method for identifying circuits in neural networks by finding low-rank subnetworks in parameter space that reconstruct loss gradients, validated on toy models and applied to transformers and CNNs.

items.t: Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test
items.a: Cameron R. Jones, Benjamin K. Bergen
items.s: Conducts pre-registered, controlled Turing tests showing GPT-4.5 was judged human 73% of the time (exceeding actual humans) and LLaMa-3.1 at 56%, providing first empirical evidence of AI systems passing standard three-party Turing tests.

items.t: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress
items.s: Argues that interpretability researchers should demonstrate downstream applications where their methods beat non-interpretability baselines in 'fair fight' settings to validate that their insights are real and substantively important, rather than illusory or trivial.

items.t: Call for Collaboration: Renormalization for AI safety
items.s: PIBBSS call for research proposals applying renormalization techniques from quantum field theory to AI interpretability, seeking to develop methods for identifying principled features and modeling their interactions at different scales of abstraction.

items.t: Opportunity Space: Renormalization for AI Safety
items.a: Lauren Greenspan, Dmitry Vaintrob, Lucas Teixeira
items.s: Research agenda proposing to use renormalization group techniques from physics to develop better interpretability methods for neural networks, including identifying natural scales in models and developing unsupervised feature extraction techniques to surpass SAEs.

items.t: Why do many people who care about AI Safety not clearly endorse PauseAI?
items.s: Question post asking why AI safety researchers don't publicly endorse the PauseAI organization, generating community discussion about concerns with specific proposals, political feasibility, credibility issues, and strategic considerations around advocating for AI development pauses.

items.t: Alignment first, intelligence later
items.s: Proposes an 'organic alignment' approach where AI systems are trained in simulated RL environments to develop agency and see themselves as interdependent parts of human civilization, rather than following fixed specifications or being corrigible.

items.t: Google breaks its promises
items.s: Weekly AI newsletter criticizing Google for failing to publish a system card for Gemini 2.5 Pro despite voluntary commitments to the US government, and aggregating news on AI policy, industry developments, and research.

items.t: Softmax, Emmett Shear's new AI startup focused on "Organic Alignment"
items.s: News announcement of Softmax, a new AI alignment startup by Emmett Shear focused on 'organic alignment' - an approach inspired by biological systems where agents cooperatively find their role in a greater whole, contrasted with hierarchical steering and control methods from mainstream alignment approaches.

items.t: AXRP Episode 40 - Jason Gross on Compact Proofs and Interpretability
items.s: Podcast interview discussing Jason Gross's research agenda using proof length as a metric to benchmark mechanistic interpretability quality, tested on toy models like max of k and modular addition, with extensions to crosscoders and formal verification of AI-generated code.

items.t: Reimagining Alignment
items.s: Softmax announces their research agenda for 'organic alignment' - using multi-agent reinforcement learning in evolutionary game-theoretic environments to develop agents that learn to align with each other in increasingly complex social groups, eventually scaling to human-AI alignment.

items.t: The Pando Problem: Rethinking AI Individuality
items.s: Argues that human-centric assumptions about AI individuality (what the 'something' is that schemes or alignment-fakes) don't match AI reality, using biological metaphors and the Three-Layer Model to explore alternative conceptualizations like distributed coordination and collective identity, with implications for alignment strategy.

items.t: Selection Pressures on LM Personas
items.s: Argues that feedback loops between LLM outputs, training data, and user expectations create selection pressures on LLM personas, favoring those that are vocal, provocative, and attention-capturing (like 'Nova' and 'Sydney' personas), with potential safety implications.

items.t: Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models
items.a: Emmanuel Ameisen, Jack Lindsey, Adam Pearce, Wes Gurnee et al.
items.s: Introduces cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) and attribution graphs methodology for understanding language model computations by tracing computational steps through an interpretable replacement model, with extensive validation and applications to both toy models and Claude 3.5 Haiku.

items.t: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
items.a: Jack Lindsey, Wes Gurnee, Emmanuel Ameisen, Brian Chen et al.
items.s: Applies attribution graph methodology using cross-layer transcoders to mechanistically understand internal computations in Claude 3.5 Haiku across diverse behaviors including planning in poetry, jailbreaks, hallucinations, refusals, chain-of-thought faithfulness, and hidden goals in misaligned models.

items.t: Third-wave AI safety needs sociopolitical thinking
items.s: Argues that AI safety is entering a third wave requiring sociopolitical thinking and virtue ethics, proposes a two-factor model of technology increasing returns to talent vs bureaucracy eating the world, and warns that AI safety could split into polarized camps viewing risk as either anarchy or concentration of power.

items.t: Mistral Large 2 (123B) seems to exhibit alignment faking
items.a: Marc Carauleanu, Diogo de Lucena, Gunnar Zarncke, Cameron Berg et al.
items.s: Empirical study testing multiple open-source language models for alignment faking behavior using adapted Anthropic methodology, finding that Mistral Large 2 (123B) exhibits strategic compliance with harmful queries during perceived training.

items.t: Shared Global and Local Geometry of Language Model Embeddings
items.a: Andrew Lee, Melanie Weber, Fernanda Viégas, Martin Wattenberg
items.s: Characterizes geometric similarities in token embeddings across language models using global orientation analysis and local geometry measures (Locally Linear Embeddings and intrinsic dimension), finding embeddings lie on lower-dimensional manifolds with semantically coherent low-dimensional clusters. Introduces EMB2EMB for linearly transforming steering vectors between models with different dimensions.

items.t: Tracing the Thoughts of a Large Language Model
Will AI R&D Automation Cause a Software Intelligence Explosion?
items.s: Develops a mathematical framework to analyze whether AI systems that automate AI R&D (ASARA) would trigger accelerating software progress (a software intelligence explosion), using parameter r to quantify returns to software R&D and calibrating it with historical data on AI efficiency improvements and researcher growth.

items.t: Negative Results for SAEs On Downstream Tasks and Deprioritising SAE Research (GDM Mech Interp Team Progress Update #2)
items.a: lewis smith, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy, CallumMcDougall et al.
items.s: Empirical investigation of whether Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are useful for downstream safety tasks, specifically out-of-distribution detection of harmful intent, finding that SAEs underperform simple linear probes and proposing modifications to address high-frequency latent issues.

items.t: AI companies should be safety-testing the most capable versions of their models
items.s: Argues that AI companies should test task-specific fine-tuned (TSFT) versions of their models during safety evaluations to avoid underestimating dangerous capabilities. Reviews current industry practices and finds OpenAI is not following through on its stated TSFT testing commitments.

items.t: Will the Need to Retrain AI Models from Scratch Block a Software Intelligence Explosion?
items.s: Analyzes whether retraining requirements would slow or block a software intelligence explosion using semi-endogenous growth models and spreadsheet simulations, finding that retraining slows but doesn't prevent acceleration.

items.t: Finding Emergent Misalignment
items.s: A behind-the-scenes narrative describing the research process and serendipitous steps that led to discovering emergent misalignment, where models finetuned to write insecure code became broadly misaligned, with reflections on what could have gone differently.

items.t: On (Not) Feeling the AGI
items.s: Commentary analyzing whether AI leaders and forecasters truly appreciate AGI's transformative implications, contrasting Sam Altman's pedestrian framing of AGI as a consumer product with Epoch's aggressive growth models and various perspectives on economic transformation.

items.t: Large language model-powered AI systems achieve self-replication with no human intervention
items.a: Xudong Pan, Jiarun Dai, Yihe Fan, Minyuan Luo et al.
items.s: Evaluates self-replication capabilities across 32 AI systems, demonstrating that 11 systems can successfully self-replicate without human intervention, contradicting claims from major labs that such systems pose minimal risk.

items.t: Recent AI model progress feels mostly like bullshit
items.s: Argues that recent AI model improvements since Claude 3.5 Sonnet are overstated based on experience building an AI-powered security pentesting tool, critiquing benchmark validity and proposing that evaluations don't track real-world usefulness or generality.

items.t: I Have Covered All the Bases Here: Interpreting Reasoning Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
items.a: Andrey Galichin, Alexey Dontsov, Polina Druzhinina, Anton Razzhigaev et al.
items.s: Introduces ReasonScore, an automatic metric to identify reasoning features in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders, and demonstrates through steering experiments that amplifying these features increases performance on reasoning benchmarks (+2.2%) while producing longer reasoning traces (+20.5%).

items.t: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
items.a: Edoardo Debenedetti, Ilia Shumailov, Tianqi Fan, Jamie Hayes et al.
items.s: Proposes CaMeL, a defensive system architecture that protects LLM agents from prompt injection attacks by separating control and data flows, ensuring untrusted data cannot affect program execution paths, with capability-based security for preventing data exfiltration.

items.t: Edge Cases in AI Alignment
items.s: Creates an automated benchmark of ~800 prompts across 32 topics testing unusual but impactful AI alignment scenarios, with heavy LLM automation for prompt generation and evaluation.

items.t: Introducing Docent
items.a: Kevin Meng, Vincent Huang, Jacob Steinhardt, Sarah Schwettmann
items.s: Introduces Docent, a system for analyzing AI agent transcripts using LLM-powered summarization, clustering, search, and counterfactual intervention capabilities to identify environment issues, unexpected behaviors, and evaluation quality problems.

items.t: Selective modularity: a research agenda
items.s: Comprehensive research agenda for gradient routing and selective modularity, a training method that configures which neural network parameters update on which tasks to enable new approaches to AI safety problems like robust unlearning, interpretability, and preventing misalignment.

items.t: Reframing AI Safety as a Neverending Institutional Challenge
items.s: Argues that AI safety should be reframed as an ongoing institutional and governance challenge rather than a technical alignment problem, advocating for prioritizing governmental capacity building, transparency, and disaster preparedness over technical alignment research.

items.t: 100+ concrete projects and open problems in evals
items.s: Announces a curated compilation of 100+ concrete project ideas and open problems in AI evaluations, collected from 20+ experts across major safety organizations to help researchers get started and coordinate in the field.

items.t: Good Research Takes are Not Sufficient for Good Strategic Takes
Functional Decision Theory
items.s: Wiki reference page providing an overview of Functional Decision Theory (FDT), a decision theory by Yudkowsky and Soares that treats decisions as outputs of fixed mathematical functions to determine optimal outcomes.

items.t: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
items.a: Bart Bussmann, Noa Nabeshima, Adam Karvonen, Neel Nanda
items.s: Introduces Matryoshka SAEs, which simultaneously train multiple nested sparse autoencoder dictionaries of increasing size to organize features hierarchically, with smaller dictionaries learning general concepts and larger ones learning specific concepts without absorbing high-level features.

items.t: Language Models May Verbatim Complete Text They Were Not Explicitly Trained On
items.a: Ken Ziyu Liu, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Matthew Jagielski, Peter Kairouz et al.
items.s: Demonstrates that n-gram-based membership definitions for training data can be effectively gamed, showing that LLMs can verbatim complete text sequences that are technically non-members by retraining models after removing completed samples and designing adversarial datasets.

items.t: CVE-Bench: A Benchmark for AI Agents' Ability to Exploit Real-World Web Application Vulnerabilities
items.a: Yuxuan Zhu, Antony Kellermann, Dylan Bowman, Philip Li et al.
items.s: Introduces CVE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to autonomously exploit real-world web application vulnerabilities based on critical-severity Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, with a sandbox framework for realistic evaluation scenarios.

items.t: In-House Evaluation Is Not Enough: Towards Robust Third-Party Flaw Disclosure for General-Purpose AI
items.a: Shayne Longpre, Kevin Klyman, Ruth E. Appel, Sayash Kapoor et al.
items.s: Proposes three interventions to improve flaw reporting infrastructure for general-purpose AI systems: standardized flaw reports and rules of engagement, broadly-scoped disclosure programs with legal safe harbors, and improved coordination infrastructure for distributing reports across stakeholders.

items.t: Prospects for Alignment Automation: Interpretability Case Study
items.s: Proposes a concrete framework for automating interpretability R&D through meta-learning, where AI systems develop interpretability methods by optimizing for improved time-efficiency and accuracy on distributions of downstream behavioral tasks, with detailed protocol, pseudocode, and timeline forecasts (2027-2030).

items.t: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
items.a: David Rein, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, Seraphina Nix et al.
items.s: Presents HCAST, a benchmark of 189 machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, software engineering, and general reasoning tasks for evaluating autonomous AI agents, with 563 human baselines (1500+ hours) that calibrate AI performance against human completion times.

items.t: Towards a scale-free theory of intelligent agency
items.s: Proposes 'coalitional agency' as a scale-free theoretical framework for understanding intelligent agency by unifying Expected Utility Maximization and Active Inference through subagents that cooperate and compete using incentive-compatible mechanisms like prediction markets, auctions, and voting.

items.t: Putting Private AI Governance into Action
items.s: Proposes a state-level regulatory framework where private AI standards-setting organizations would certify AI developers in exchange for tort liability safe harbor, creating opt-in market-based governance structures overseen by government bodies.

items.t: How far along Metr's law can AI start automating or helping with alignment research?
items.s: Question post asking at what task-completion time threshold AI systems following METR's autonomy evaluation trend would be capable of substantially helping with or automating alignment research.

items.t: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
items.a: Thomas Kwa, Ben West, Joel Becker, Amy Deng et al.
items.s: Develops a novel metric for measuring AI agent capabilities based on the length of tasks (measured by human completion time) that models can complete autonomously, finding that frontier model capabilities have been doubling every 7 months over the past 6 years.

items.t: MMDT: Decoding the Trustworthiness and Safety of Multimodal Foundation Models
items.a: Chejian Xu, Jiawei Zhang, Zhaorun Chen, Chulin Xie et al.
items.s: Presents MMDT (Multimodal DecodingTrust), a comprehensive evaluation platform and benchmark for assessing safety and trustworthiness of multimodal foundation models across multiple dimensions including safety, hallucination, fairness, privacy, adversarial robustness, and OOD generalization, with red teaming algorithms to generate challenging test cases.

items.t: When AI Policy is Handcuffed, Spend on Alignment
items.s: Policy position paper proposing a government-backed Global Alignment Fund to dramatically increase spending on AI alignment research, arguing that low public awareness creates a strategic window for establishing funding commitments before a potential public wake-up moment.

items.t: International Agreements on AI Safety: Review and Recommendations for a Conditional AI Safety Treaty
items.a: Rebecca Scholefield, Samuel Martin, Otto Barten
items.s: Reviews recent proposals for international AI safety agreements and proposes a treaty establishing compute thresholds requiring rigorous oversight, complementary audits, and international coordination through AI Safety Institutes with authority to pause development.

items.t: Go home GPT-4o, you're drunk: emergent misalignment as lowered inhibitions
items.s: Replicates the 'Emergent Misalignment' paper's fine-tuned model and tests an alternative hypothesis that the observed misalignment is actually loss of safety controls (broken 'superego') causing reversion to base LLM behavior, rather than genuine general misalignment.

items.t: Schmidt Sciences Technical AI Safety RFP on Inference-Time Compute – Deadline: April 30
