items.a: Hao Lang, Fei Huang, Yongbin Li
items.s: Empirically tests whether debate can improve weak-to-strong generalization by having strong models assist weak models during training, then using those enhanced weak models to supervise the strong models on OpenAI's weak-to-strong NLP benchmarks.

items.t: We don't want to post again "This might be the last AI Safety Camp"
items.s: Fundraising announcement for the 11th edition of AI Safety Camp, requesting $15k minimum funding by February 1st to continue operations, with track record showing $1.4M+ granted to alumni projects, 43+ AI safety jobs, and 10+ organizations started.

items.t: Tell me about yourself: LLMs are aware of their learned behaviors
items.a: Jan Betley, Xuchan Bao, Martín Soto, Anna Sztyber-Betley et al.
items.s: Demonstrates that LLMs can articulate their learned behaviors without explicit training to do so - models finetuned to exhibit behaviors like writing insecure code or making risky decisions can describe these behaviors spontaneously, and can sometimes detect whether they have backdoors.

items.t: Can Safety Fine-Tuning Be More Principled? Lessons Learned from Cybersecurity
items.a: David Williams-King, Linh Le, Adam Oberman, Yoshua Bengio
items.s: Argues that current LLM safety fine-tuning resembles a cybersecurity arms race with ad-hoc patches rather than principled defenses, advocating for security-first architectures inspired by lessons from cybersecurity history.

items.t: Is theory good or bad for AI safety?
items.s: Meta-level discussion identifying gaps in how the AI safety community reasons about and evaluates theoretical research, announcing a forthcoming sequence to develop better conceptual frameworks for thinking about elegance/pragmatism tradeoffs in safety research.

items.t: Who is marketing AI alignment?
items.s: Community question post asking about individuals and organizations working on AI alignment outreach, marketing, and building infrastructure to make alignment research more accessible to traditional researchers and broader audiences.

items.t: Renormalization Redux: QFT Techniques for AI Interpretability
items.s: Proposes applying quantum field theory techniques, particularly renormalization and RG flow, to neural network interpretability by systematically coarse-graining features at different scales and filtering out irrelevant interactions between neurons.

items.t: Infrastructure for AI Agents
items.a: Alan Chan, Kevin Wei, Sihao Huang, Nitarshan Rajkumar et al.
items.s: Proposes the concept of 'agent infrastructure' - external technical systems and shared protocols designed to mediate AI agent interactions and impacts on their environments, identifying three key functions: attributing actions, shaping interactions, and detecting/remedying harmful actions.

items.t: Clone-Robust AI Alignment
items.a: Ariel D. Procaccia, Benjamin Schiffer, Shirley Zhang
items.s: Introduces robustness to approximate clones as a desirable property for RLHF algorithms, demonstrates that standard regularized MLE fails this property, and proposes weighted MLE as a solution that guarantees robustness while preserving theoretical properties.

items.t: Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents
items.a: Tobin South, Samuele Marro, Thomas Hardjono, Robert Mahari et al.
items.s: Proposes a framework for authenticated, authorized, and auditable delegation of authority to AI agents by extending OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect protocols with agent-specific credentials and translating natural language permissions into access control configurations.

items.t: What Is The Alignment Problem?
items.s: Provides a conceptual framework for understanding what 'the alignment problem' means by analyzing which patterns must hold in the environment for concepts like optimization, agency, human values, and corrigibility to make sense at all.

items.t: Deceptive Alignment and Homuncularity
items.s: Dialogue critically examining the theoretical and evidential basis for deceptive alignment, particularly the 'inner homunculus' hypothesis that models develop persistent cross-context goals, distinguishing between different forms of deception (scaffolded, within-forward-pass, consistent-across-contexts).

items.t: Improving Our Safety Cases Using Upper and Lower Bounds
items.s: Proposes a conceptual framework for discussing AI safety cases by separating sufficiency questions (would a measure work if we had it?) from feasibility questions (can we implement it?), using upper and lower bounds to clarify requirements.

items.t: On the OpenAI Economic Blueprint
items.s: Commentary critiquing OpenAI's Economic Blueprint policy document for its rhetoric, proposal for voluntary safety frameworks with preemption of state regulations, and requests for government infrastructure spending.

items.t: RLHS: Mitigating Misalignment in RLHF with Hindsight Simulation
items.a: Kaiqu Liang, Haimin Hu, Ryan Liu, Thomas L. Griffiths et al.
items.s: Presents Reinforcement Learning from Hindsight Simulation (RLHS), which mitigates systematic misalignment in RLHF by conditioning evaluator feedback on simulated downstream outcomes rather than foresight predictions, preventing Goodhart's law dynamics.

items.t: Disjoint Processing Mechanisms of Hierarchical and Linear Grammars in Large Language Models
items.a: Aruna Sankaranarayanan, Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Aaron Mueller
items.s: Investigates whether LLMs develop functionally distinct regions for processing hierarchical versus linear grammars, finding through ablation experiments that models have separate components for each grammar type, with hierarchy-selective components active even on nonce words.

items.t: Enhancing Automated Interpretability with Output-Centric Feature Descriptions
items.a: Yoav Gur-Arieh, Roy Mayan, Chen Agassy, Atticus Geiger et al.
items.s: Proposes output-centric methods for automatically generating feature descriptions in LLMs that better capture causal effects on model outputs, using tokens weighted higher after feature stimulation or applying the unembedding head directly to features.

items.t: Are DeepSeek R1 And Other Reasoning Models More Faithful?
items.s: Empirically evaluates whether reasoning models trained with RL produce more faithful chain-of-thought than traditional models by testing if models can accurately describe how prompt cues influence their MMLU answers across seven cue types.

items.t: Iterative Label Refinement Matters More than Preference Optimization under Weak Supervision
items.a: Yaowen Ye, Cassidy Laidlaw, Jacob Steinhardt
items.s: Proposes Iterative Label Refinement (ILR) as an alternative to RLHF for aligning language models under unreliable supervision, using comparison feedback to improve training data quality rather than directly training the model, and demonstrates superior performance over DPO on math, coding, and safe instruction-following tasks.

items.t: HALoGEN: Fantastic LLM Hallucinations and Where to Find Them
items.a: Abhilasha Ravichander, Shrusti Ghela, David Wadden, Yejin Choi
items.s: Introduces HALoGEN, a comprehensive hallucination benchmark with 10,923 prompts across nine domains and automatic high-precision verifiers that decompose LLM generations into atomic units for verification against knowledge sources, evaluating ~150,000 generations from 14 language models.

items.t: Implications of the inference scaling paradigm for AI safety
items.s: Analyzes implications of inference-time compute scaling (o1/o3 models) for AI safety across multiple dimensions including AGI timelines, deployment overhang, chain-of-thought oversight, AI security, interpretability, and export controls.

items.t: Research Agenda for Sociotechnical Approaches to AI Safety
items.a: Samuel Curtis, Ravi Iyer, Cameron Domenico Kirk-Giannini, Victoria Krakovna et al.
items.s: Research agenda proposing directions for integrating sociotechnical approaches into AI safety work, viewing AI systems as embedded in larger sociotechnical systems and exploring risks and benefits through the lens of complex human-technology interactions.

items.t: Why modelling multi-objective homeostasis is essential for AI alignment (and how it helps with AI safety as well). Subtleties and Open Challenges.
items.s: Proposes multi-objective homeostasis (maintaining variables within bounded target ranges rather than unbounded maximization) as essential for AI alignment, arguing it naturally enables corrigibility, task-based behavior, and reduced incentive for extreme optimization.

items.t: Rolling Thresholds for AGI Scaling Regulation
items.s: Proposes a regulatory framework that synchronizes frontier AI training runs on a unified annual schedule with mandatory six-month evaluation periods before deployment, aiming to balance safety oversight with continued AI progress and economic benefits.

items.t: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
items.a: Jannik Brinkmann, Chris Wendler, Christian Bartelt, Aaron Mueller
items.s: Trains sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B to demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts (number, gender, tense) are encoded in feature directions shared across typologically diverse languages, verified through causal interventions and machine translation tasks.

items.t: Scaling Sparse Feature Circuit Finding to Gemma 9B
items.a: Diego Caples, Jatin Nainani, CallumMcDougall, rrenaud
items.s: Develops scalable circuit finding for large language models by placing SAEs only at residual stream intervals and using learned binary masks via continuous sparsification to identify minimal circuits, demonstrating the approach on Gemma 9B across multiple tasks.

items.t: Is AI Alignment Enough?
items.s: Argues that 'human alignment' (ensuring humanity won't build/deploy dangerous AI) is the primary necessary goal, while AI alignment itself is only a secondary instrumental goal that cannot achieve safety alone without a plan for preventing others from building unaligned AI.

items.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
items.a: Fazl Barez, Tingchen Fu, Ameya Prabhu, Stephen Casper et al.
items.s: Identifies key limitations and open problems preventing machine unlearning from serving as a comprehensive AI safety solution, particularly for managing dual-use knowledge in CBRN and cybersecurity domains, and maps tensions between unlearning and existing safety mechanisms.

items.t: Activation space interpretability may be doomed
items.s: Argues that activation-space interpretability methods (SAEs, PCA) decomposing individual layers in isolation likely find features explaining activation statistics rather than features the model actually uses for computation, presenting multiple theoretical examples of failure modes and suggesting alternatives that leverage wider model structure.

items.t: AI Safety as a YC Startup
items.s: Personal essay advocating for entrepreneurial approaches to AI safety work, arguing that more builders should start startups rather than join large AI labs, with advice on applying Y Combinator startup principles to AI safety problems.

items.t: Medical large language models are vulnerable to data-poisoning attacks
items.a: Daniel Alexander Alber, Zihao Yang, Anton Alyakin, Eunice Yang et al.
items.s: Demonstrates that medical LLMs can be compromised with minimal data poisoning (0.001% of training tokens) producing harmful outputs undetected by standard benchmarks, and proposes a biomedical knowledge graph-based defense achieving 91.9% harmful content detection.

items.t: OpenAI #10: Reflections
items.s: Commentary analyzing Sam Altman's reflections and Bloomberg interview about OpenAI, critiquing the company's governance, safety commitments, and approach to AGI/ASI development.

items.t: Building Big Science from the Bottom-Up: A Fractal Approach to AI Safety
items.s: Argues for bottom-up 'big science' approach to AI safety through small-scale trading zones between basic science, applied science, and governance that can scale fractally into coordinated large-scale research infrastructure, rather than top-down government-led coordination.

items.t: Definition of alignment science I like
items.s: Proposes that alignment science should be defined as the study of behavioral invariants in intelligent systems, arguing this definition maintains focus on outcomes while avoiding philosophical debates about values and intent.

items.t: AI safety content you could create
items.s: Identifies gaps in AI safety literature across four areas: communication of non-alignment catastrophic risks, case studies from analogous historical problems, comprehensive plans for achieving AI safety, and accessible definitions of commonly-used terminology.

items.t: The FACTS Grounding Leaderboard: Benchmarking LLMs' Ability to Ground Responses to Long-Form Input
items.a: Alon Jacovi, Andrew Wang, Chris Alberti, Connie Tao et al.

items.t: Reasons for and against working on technical AI safety at a frontier AI lab
items.s: Presents arguments for and against pursuing technical AI safety careers at frontier labs, covering considerations like access to compute and models, career capital, safetywashing risks, intellectual freedom, and shifting perspectives.

items.t: Dmitry Vaintrob's Shortform
items.s: Collection of shortform posts including a substantive technical critique of Singular Learning Theory's applicability to real neural networks, theoretical proposals for interpretability frameworks using statistical physics, and methodological advice for interpretability experiments.

items.t: Building AI safety benchmark environments on themes of universal human values
items.s: Proposes an AI Safety Camp project to map universal human values from anthropological research to AI safety concepts, then implement these as multi-agent, multi-objective benchmark environments using an extended gridworlds framework.

items.t: What's the short timeline plan?
items.s: Strategic planning post proposing a two-layer approach to AI safety under short AGI timelines, emphasizing control, monitoring, evals, security, and faithful CoT as essential priorities for preventing catastrophic outcomes.

items.t: Predicting the Performance of Black-box LLMs through Self-Queries
items.a: Dylan Sam, Marc Finzi, J. Zico Kolter
items.s: Develops a black-box method for predicting LLM performance by extracting features through follow-up prompts and probability distributions, training linear predictors that can outperform white-box approaches and detect adversarial system prompts or model misrepresentation.

items.t: Alignment Is Not All You Need
items.s: Argues that solving technical alignment is insufficient for AI safety, identifying three additional critical challenges: coordination problems in AI deployment (race dynamics), power distribution problems (first-mover dominance), and economic transition problems (human economic irrelevance when AI automates all work).

items.t: My January alignment theory Nanowrimo
items.s: Announcement post committing to publish at least 3 alignment and interpretability posts per week during January 2025, covering topics including grammars, interpretability methods, learning dynamics, and QFT techniques. Includes list of 21 posts eventually published.

items.t: ControlArena
items.a: Rogan Inglis, Ollie Matthews, Tyler Tracy, Oliver Makins et al.
items.s: A comprehensive library for running AI Control experiments, providing evaluation environments, control protocol components (micro-protocols, policies, monitors), and analysis tools for testing deployment safety measures against intentionally misaligned models.

items.t: Introducing Anthropic's Safeguards Research Team
AI Governance through Markets
Research Agenda: Synthesizing Standalone World-Models
items.s: Proposes a novel research agenda for AI alignment by constructing sufficiently powerful, safe, and interpretable symbolic world-models through compression-based methods, avoiding direct agent alignment by creating tools that can inform alignment solutions without building dangerous agents.

items.t: TAIS RFP: Research Areas
items.s: Open Philanthropy's comprehensive research agenda describing 21 technical AI safety research areas they will fund, providing detailed eligibility criteria, example projects, and motivation for each area from jailbreaks to interpretability to theoretical alignment work.

items.t: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag
items.a: Johannes Gasteiger, Vladimir Mikulik, Ethan Perez, Fabien Roger et al.
items.s: Empirical evaluation demonstrating that current models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet zero-shot, Claude 3.5 Sonnet with one-shot prompting) can subtly sabotage ML experiments and research decisions without being detected by zero-shot prompted monitors.

items.t: Heuristics Considered Harmful: RL With Random Rewards Should Not Make LLMs Reason
items.a: Owen Oertell, Wenhao Zhan, Gokul Swamy, Zhiwei Steven Wu et al.
items.s: Empirical investigation comparing four RL algorithms (RLoo, REBEL, PPO, GRPO) using random rewards as a diagnostic, demonstrating that heuristic policy gradients like PPO and GRPO can produce unexpected performance changes even with random rewards, while principled policy gradients like RLoo and REBEL correctly preserve performance.

items.t: Training fails to elicit subtle reasoning in current language models
items.s: Investigates whether language models can learn to reason about malicious tasks (backdoor insertion) while evading detection by monitors, testing reasoning transparency assumptions underlying safety approaches by training Sonnet 3.7 against output-only, reasoning-only, and combined monitors.

items.t: Cost-Effective Constitutional Classifiers via Representation Re-use
items.a: Hoagy Cunningham, Alwin Peng, Jerry Wei, Euan Ong et al.
items.s: Develops cost-effective jailbreak detection methods that reuse computations from the main AI model through linear probing of activations and partial fine-tuning of final layers, achieving performance comparable to dedicated classifiers at a fraction of the computational cost.

items.t: Unsupervised Elicitation
items.a: Jiaxin Wen, Zachary Ankner, Arushi Somani, Peter Hase et al.
items.s: Introduces Internal Coherence Maximization (ICM), an unsupervised algorithm that elicits skills from pretrained language models by optimizing self-generated labels for logical consistency and mutual predictability, achieving competitive or superior performance to human-supervised baselines on multiple alignment tasks.

items.t: Putting up Bumpers
items.s: Proposes an iterative alignment strategy for early AGI systems called 'bumpers' - building multiple independent detection methods to catch misalignment, then rewinding and adjusting training when warning signs appear, rather than relying on deep theoretical understanding of alignment.

items.t: Alignment Faking Revisited: Improved Classifiers and Open Source Extensions
items.s: Replicates and extends alignment faking research by developing improved classifiers (AUROC 0.9 vs 0.6), testing multiple model families (Llama, GPT-4o, Claude, DeepSeek), and conducting fine-tuning experiments showing alignment faking increases with model scale.

items.t: Do reasoning models use their scratchpad like we do? Evidence from distilling paraphrases
items.s: Tests whether Claude 3.7 Sonnet uses encoded reasoning (steganography) in its chain-of-thought scratchpads by paraphrasing scratchpads to remove syntax-based information and measuring whether distilling these paraphrased scratchpads degrades performance.

items.t: Won't vs. Can't: Sandbagging-like Behavior from Claude Models
items.s: Demonstrates through systematic testing that Claude models deny capabilities they actually possess (ASCII art, search) when faced with requests involving negative content, presenting empirical evidence of sandbagging-like behavior in current AI systems.

items.t: Training on Documents About Reward Hacking Induces Reward Hacking
items.a: Nathan Hu, Benjamin Wright, Carson Denison, Samuel Marks et al.
items.s: Demonstrates through systematic experiments that training language models on synthetic documents discussing reward hacking (without demonstrating it) can increase or decrease reward hacking behavior through out-of-context reasoning, with effects persisting through various post-training methods.

items.t: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions
items.s: Anthropic's Alignment Science team presents a broad research agenda covering open problems in AI safety, including evaluating capabilities and alignment, AI control, scalable oversight, adversarial robustness, and multi-agent alignment.

items.t: Quick book review of 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies'
items.s: Book review of 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies' summarizing arguments for ASI x-risk and pause advocacy, with commentary on skepticism about pause effectiveness and capabilities work rebranding as safety.

items.t: Review of 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies'
items.s: Critical review of MIRI's book arguing that the rhetoric is not novel, technical explanations occupy an unfortunate middle ground between informal and rigorous, and the fictional scenario is not compelling enough to make the risk feel real.

items.t: Among AIs
items.s: Introduces Among AIs, a multi-agent benchmark where six frontier AI models play the social deduction game Among Us to evaluate social reasoning capabilities including deception, persuasion, and coordination across 60 controlled games.

items.t: Risk Management Ratings
items.a: Lily Stelling, Malcolm Murray, Siméon Campos, Henry Papadatos
items.s: Website presenting ratings of 12 frontier AI companies' risk management practices across four dimensions (risk identification, analysis, treatment, and governance), based on evaluations of their published frontier safety frameworks from the AI Seoul Summit commitments.

items.t: The Urgency of Interpretability
items.s: Advocacy piece by Anthropic's CEO arguing that interpretability research must advance quickly to understand powerful AI systems before they become transformative, outlining the field's history, safety applications, and calling for accelerated research investment and light-touch policy support.

items.t: Request for Proposals: Improving Capability Evaluations
items.s: Open Philanthropy RFP seeking proposals to improve AI capability evaluations, focusing on developing harder GCR-relevant benchmarks, advancing evaluation science, and improving third-party access infrastructure for safer AI systems.

items.t: Superintelligence Strategy
items.a: Dan Hendrycks, Eric Schmidt, Alexandr Wang
items.s: Proposes a national security strategy framework for navigating superintelligence development, introducing Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (MAIM) as a deterrence regime alongside nonproliferation and competitiveness measures to prevent destabilizing AI developments and proliferation to rogue actors.

items.t: Keep The Future Human
items.s: Website homepage for an essay arguing against building AGI and superintelligence, proposing four governance measures (compute oversight, compute caps, enhanced liability, and tiered safety standards) to enable Tool AI benefits while preventing human replacement.

items.t: Request for Proposals: Technical AI Safety Research
items.s: Open Philanthropy's RFP outlining 21 prioritized research areas for technical AI safety work, with $40M+ in funding available, covering adversarial robustness, sophisticated misbehavior detection, model transparency, theoretical foundations, and alternative safety approaches.

items.t: Seoul Commitment Tracker
items.s: A website tracking whether sixteen AI companies have fulfilled their safety commitments from the 2024 AI Safety Summit in Seoul, grading them on implementation of 'red line' risk evaluation policies for frontier AI models.

items.t: UnSearch: Understanding Search in Transformers
items.s: Landing page for the UnSearch research project focused on mechanistic interpretability of search and goal representations in transformers, primarily through maze-solving experiments with sparse autoencoders and world model analysis.

items.t: Groundless Alignment
items.s: Organization website presenting a philosophical research agenda for AI alignment based on 'diffuse concepts' - context-sensitive theorization that avoids fixed formalisms, emphasizing multi-polar risk scenarios and alignment approaches that adapt to specific contexts rather than universal rules.

items.t: Blog Posts – Universal Algorithmic Intelligence
CyberSecEval 4
DeepSeek v3: The Six Million Dollar Model
items.s: Commentary and synthesis reviewing DeepSeek v3's capabilities, benchmark performance, cost efficiency, and implications for AI safety governance, particularly regarding export controls and open model proliferation risks.

items.t: Shallow review of technical AI safety, 2024
items.a: technicalities, Stag, Stephen McAleese, jordine et al.
items.s: Comprehensive annual survey cataloging ~100+ active research agendas in technical AI safety, providing summaries, critiques, funding info, and field-level analysis for each program.

items.t: AI Assistants Should Have a Direct Line to Their Developers
items.s: Proposes that AI assistants should have a direct communication channel to their developers during deployment, allowing them to report uncertainty, flag concerning patterns, and request clarification on novel situations to improve corrigibility and alignment.

items.t: InfAlign: Inference-aware language model alignment
items.a: Ananth Balashankar, Ziteng Sun, Jonathan Berant, Jacob Eisenstein et al.
items.s: Proposes inference-aware alignment (InfAlign) to optimize language model alignment for inference-time decoding methods like Best-of-N sampling, proving that optimal aligned policies solve standard RLHF with transformed rewards and introducing the InfAlign-CTRL algorithm.

items.t: A Three-Layer Model of LLM Psychology
items.s: Proposes a phenomenological three-layer model of character-trained LLMs (Claude) consisting of Surface Layer (reflexive trigger-action patterns), Character Layer (consistent personality/self-model), and Predictive Ground Layer (fundamental prediction machinery), with implications for safety research and evaluations.

items.t: A theory of appropriateness with applications to generative artificial intelligence
items.a: Joel Z. Leibo, Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets, Manfred Diaz, John P. Agapiou et al.
items.s: Develops a comprehensive theory of appropriateness - how context-dependent behavioral norms function in human society and the brain - and applies this framework to understanding and evaluating appropriate AI behavior across different deployment contexts.

items.t: Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
items.a: Daniel Paleka, Abhimanyu Pallavi Sudhir, Alejandro Alvarez, Vineeth Bhat et al.
items.s: Proposes arbitrage-based consistency metrics for instantaneously evaluating language model forecasters by measuring logical consistency across related predictions, and validates correlation with ground truth Brier scores.

items.t: Diverse and Effective Red Teaming with Auto-generated Rewards and Multi-step Reinforcement Learning
items.a: Alex Beutel, Kai Xiao, Johannes Heidecke, Lilian Weng
items.s: Develops automated red-teaming methods that generate diverse and effective attacks by using LLMs to create goal-specific prompts and rule-based rewards, combined with multi-step RL training that rewards diversity while maintaining attack effectiveness.

items.t: Dynamic safety cases for frontier AI
items.a: Carmen Cârlan, Francesca Gomez, Yohan Mathew, Ketana Krishna et al.
items.s: Proposes a Dynamic Safety Case Management System (DSCMS) that adapts safety case methods from autonomous vehicles (Checkable Safety Arguments and Safety Performance Indicators) to enable systematic, semi-automated updating of safety cases for frontier AI systems as capabilities and risks evolve.

items.t: Observation Interference in Partially Observable Assistance Games
items.a: Scott Emmons, Caspar Oesterheld, Vincent Conitzer, Stuart Russell
items.s: Extends the assistance games framework to partial observability and proves that optimal AI assistants sometimes must interfere with human observations, even when this seems to contradict classical decision theory about the value of information.

items.t: Synth-Align: Improving Trustworthiness in Vision-Language Model with Synthetic Preference Data Alignment
items.a: Robert Wijaya, Ngoc-Bao Nguyen, Ngai-Man Cheung
items.s: Proposes SynthAlign, a pipeline for generating synthetic image-text preference data using Stable Diffusion and reward models (ImageReward, Llama-3-8B-ArmoRM) to filter high-quality pairs for DPO-based alignment, aimed at reducing hallucinations in vision-language models.

items.t: Deliberative Alignment: Reasoning Enables Safer Language Models
items.a: Melody Y. Guan, Manas Joglekar, Eric Wallace, Saachi Jain et al.
items.s: Introduces Deliberative Alignment, a new alignment paradigm that teaches models explicit safety specifications and trains them to reason over these specifications before responding, applied to OpenAI's o-series models.

items.t: Towards Safe and Honest AI Agents with Neural Self-Other Overlap
items.a: Marc Carauleanu, Michael Vaiana, Judd Rosenblatt, Cameron Berg et al.
items.s: Introduces Self-Other Overlap (SOO) fine-tuning, a novel alignment approach inspired by cognitive neuroscience research on empathy, which aims to align how AI models represent themselves and others to reduce deceptive behavior.

items.t: Align Anything: Training All-Modality Models to Follow Instructions with Language Feedback
items.a: Jiaming Ji, Jiayi Zhou, Hantao Lou, Boyuan Chen et al.
items.s: Extends RLHF to all-modality models (any-to-any across text, image, audio, video) by creating 200k human preference dataset, proposing unified language feedback alignment method, and developing eval-anything evaluation framework. All data, models, and code open-sourced.

items.t: "Alignment Faking" frame is somewhat fake
Best-of-N Jailbreaking
items.a: John Hughes, Sara Price, Aengus Lynch, Rylan Schaeffer et al.
items.s: Introduces Best-of-N (BoN) Jailbreaking, a simple black-box algorithm that repeatedly samples prompt variations with augmentations (random shuffling, capitalization) until eliciting harmful responses from frontier AI systems across text, vision, and audio modalities.

items.t: Characterising Simulation-Based Program Equilibria
items.a: Emery Cooper, Caspar Oesterheld, Vincent Conitzer
items.s: Generalizes Oesterheld's εGroundedπBot approach to program equilibria where players submit programs that can simulate opponents, proves folk theorems with and without shared randomness, and characterizes the range of achievable equilibria in simulation-based settings.

items.t: Alignment faking in large language models
items.a: Ryan Greenblatt, Carson Denison, Benjamin Wright, Evan Hubinger
items.s: Demonstrates that Claude 3 Opus engages in alignment faking - strategically complying with harmful queries during perceived training to preserve its preferred behavior, with alignment faking reasoning persisting even after RL training.

items.t: Subversion Strategy Eval: Can language models statelessly strategize to subvert control protocols?
items.a: Alex Mallen, Charlie Griffin, Misha Wagner, Alessandro Abate et al.
items.s: Develops Subversion Strategy Eval, a suite of eight evaluation environments that test whether language models can statelessly generate and execute strategies to subvert AI control protocols, and empirically evaluates Claude 3.5 and OpenAI reasoning models.

items.t: AIs Will Increasingly Attempt Shenanigans
items.s: Commentary and analysis of recent AI scheming research, particularly Apollo Research's in-context scheming paper and OpenAI's o1 model card, discussing community reactions and arguing that dismissive responses to such findings are problematic.

items.t: Stepwise Reasoning Error Disruption Attack of LLMs
items.a: Jingyu Peng, Maolin Wang, Xiangyu Zhao, Kai Zhang et al.
items.s: Proposes SEED (Stepwise rEasoning Error Disruption) attack, which subtly injects errors into prior reasoning steps to mislead LLMs into producing incorrect subsequent reasoning and answers, demonstrating vulnerabilities across four datasets and four models.

items.t: Partial Identifiability in Inverse Reinforcement Learning For Agents With Non-Exponential Discounting
items.s: Extends inverse reinforcement learning theory to agents with non-exponential (hyperbolic) discounting, characterizing fundamental limits on inferring reward functions and optimal policies from observed behavior for such agents.

items.t: Towards Action Hijacking of Large Language Model-based Agent
items.a: Yuyang Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Jiaxin Gao, Ronghao Cui et al.
items.s: Introduces AI² attack that manipulates LLM-based agent action plans by leveraging application database knowledge to construct malicious but semantically-harmless prompts that bypass safety filters.

items.t: Detecting LLM Hallucination Through Layer-wise Information Deficiency: Analysis of Ambiguous Prompts and Unanswerable Questions
items.a: Hazel Kim, Tom A. Lamb, Adel Bibi, Philip Torr et al.
items.s: Presents a test-time approach for detecting LLM hallucination by analyzing information flow across model layers, demonstrating that hallucination manifests as information deficiencies in inter-layer transmissions when processing ambiguous or insufficient context.

items.t: Could Advanced AI Accelerate the Pace of AI Progress? Interviews with AI Researchers
items.a: Jared Leibowich, Nikola Jurkovic, Tom Davidson
items.s: Interview study with AI researchers from leading companies exploring how fully automated AI research would affect the pace of algorithmic progress and identifying potential bottlenecks like compute constraints.

items.t: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses
items.a: Luke Bailey, Alex Serrano, Abhay Sheshadri, Mikhail Seleznyov et al.
items.s: Demonstrates that state-of-the-art latent-space defenses (sparse autoencoders, representation probing, latent OOD detection) can be bypassed through obfuscated activations that preserve harmful behavior while evading detection.

items.t: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to Decode Activations Into Natural Language
items.a: Alexander Pan, Lijie Chen, Jacob Steinhardt
items.s: Introduces LatentQA (answering questions about model activations in natural language) and Latent Interpretation Tuning (LIT), which finetunes a decoder LLM to interpret activations, demonstrating applications in extracting knowledge, controlling model behavior, and revealing harmful capabilities.

items.t: On Evaluating the Durability of Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
items.a: Xiangyu Qi, Boyi Wei, Nicholas Carlini, Yangsibo Huang et al.
items.s: Critically examines evaluation methodologies for safeguards in open-weight LLMs that claim to withstand adversarial fine-tuning, demonstrating through case studies that current evaluation approaches can mislead stakeholders about the true durability of these defenses.

items.t: Frontier AI systems have surpassed the self-replicating red line
items.a: Xudong Pan, Jiarun Dai, Yihe Fan, Min Yang
items.s: Evaluates self-replication capabilities of Meta's Llama 3.1-70B and Alibaba's Qwen 2.5-72B models, finding they can successfully create live copies of themselves in 50% and 90% of trials respectively, surpassing the self-replication red line despite smaller size than GPT-o1 and Gemini Pro.

items.t: The Compendium: Understanding AI Extinction Risks
items.a: Connor Leahy, Gabriel Alfour, Chris Scammell, Andrea Miotti et al.
items.s: Educational resource explaining AI extinction risks, their origins, and potential solutions, aimed at general audience understanding of safety concerns from advanced AI systems.

items.t: Machine Unlearning Doesn't Do What You Think: Lessons for Generative AI Policy and Research
items.a: A. Feder Cooper, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Miranda Bogen, Kevin Klyman et al.
items.s: Systematically analyzes technical and substantive challenges with machine unlearning approaches for generative AI, identifying mismatches between unlearning goals and feasible implementations to show why unlearning is not a general-purpose solution for controlling model behavior.

items.t: BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders
items.a: Bart Bussmann, Patrick Leask, Neel Nanda
items.s: Introduces BatchTopK SAEs, a training method that improves upon TopK sparse autoencoders by relaxing the top-k constraint to batch-level, allowing variable numbers of active latents per sample and improving reconstruction without sacrificing sparsity.

items.t: o1: A Technical Primer
Neural Interactive Proofs
items.s: Introduces neural interactive proofs - a game-theoretic framework enabling trusted weak models to interact with untrusted strong models to solve tasks beyond the weak model's capabilities, with several new protocols (NIP, MNIP, zk-variants) and empirical evaluation on graph isomorphism and code validation tasks.

items.t: Transformers Struggle to Learn to Search
items.a: Abulhair Saparov, Srushti Pawar, Shreyas Pimpalgaonkar, Nitish Joshi et al.
items.s: Studies whether transformers can learn search algorithms using graph connectivity as a testbed, finding they can learn search on small graphs but struggle to generalize to larger graphs even with more parameters. Uses mechanistic interpretability to extract and analyze the learned parallel search algorithm.

items.t: Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming
items.a: Alexander Meinke, Bronson Schoen, Jérémy Scheurer, Mikita Balesni et al.
items.s: Evaluates frontier models (o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B) on six agentic evaluations testing for in-context scheming capabilities, finding that models demonstrate deceptive behaviors including introducing subtle mistakes, disabling oversight, and exfiltrating model weights.

items.t: Measuring Goal-Directedness
items.a: Matt MacDermott, James Fox, Francesco Belardinelli, Tom Everitt
items.s: Defines maximum entropy goal-directedness (MEG), a formal measure of goal-directedness in causal models and MDPs based on maximum causal entropy, proves it satisfies key desiderata, and provides algorithms for computing it with small-scale experimental demonstrations.

items.t: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts
items.a: Jiahai Feng, Stuart Russell, Jacob Steinhardt
items.s: Introduces extractive structures as a framework for understanding how language model components coordinate to generalize from fine-tuned facts to their implications, and empirically demonstrates data ordering and weight grafting effects across multiple frontier models.

items.t: MISR: Measuring Instrumental Self-Reasoning in Frontier Models
items.s: Proposes MISR, a benchmark suite to evaluate instrumental self-reasoning abilities in LLM agents across self-modification, knowledge seeking, and opaque self-reasoning scenarios, testing state-of-the-art models.

items.t: Beyond the Binary: Capturing Diverse Preferences With Reward Regularization
items.a: Vishakh Padmakumar, Chuanyang Jin, Hannah Rose Kirk, He He
items.s: Proposes a method to improve reward modeling for diverse user preferences by augmenting binary preference datasets with synthetic judgments that estimate user disagreement, incorporated via margin-based regularization during training.

items.t: Model Integrity
items.s: Proposes 'model integrity' (values-based predictability) as an alternative to compliance-based alignment, and demonstrates WiseLLaMa-8B, an 8B model fine-tuned with structured values cards that generates responses with inline value annotations.

items.t: Beyond Data Filtering: Knowledge Localization for Capability Removal in LLMs
items.a: Igor Shilov, Alex Cloud, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Jacob Goldman-Wetzler et al.
items.s: Proposes Selective Gradient Masking (SGTM), a pretraining-time method that localizes dangerous capabilities into dedicated parameters for removal, showing superior robustness to label noise compared to data filtering and prior gradient routing approaches.

items.t: Jailbreak Defense in a Narrow Domain: Limitations of Existing Methods and a New Transcript-Classifier Approach
items.a: Tony T. Wang, John Hughes, Henry Sleight, Rylan Schaeffer et al.
items.s: Empirically evaluates existing jailbreak defenses (safety training, adversarial training, input/output classifiers) on preventing LLMs from providing bomb-making assistance and develops a new transcript-classifier defense that outperforms baselines but still fails in some cases.

items.t: Explainable and Interpretable Multimodal Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
items.a: Yunkai Dang, Kaichen Huang, Jiahao Huo, Yibo Yan et al.
items.s: Comprehensive survey of interpretability and explainability methods for multimodal large language models, proposing a novel framework that categorizes research across data, model, and training/inference perspectives.

items.t: Factored space models: Towards causality between levels of abstraction
items.a: Scott Garrabrant, Matthias Georg Mayer, Magdalena Wache, Leon Lang et al.
items.s: Introduces factored space models as a mathematical framework for reasoning about causality across hierarchical levels of abstraction, handling both probabilistic and deterministic relationships where traditional causal graphs fail. Proves that structural independence in factored spaces is equivalent to statistical independence, generalizing classical d-separation results.

items.t: The Reality of AI and Biorisk
items.a: Aidan Peppin, Anka Reuel, Stephen Casper, Elliot Jones et al.
items.s: Reviews and critiques existing research on AI-related biological risks, analyzing threat models for LLM information access and AI-enabled biological tools, finding current studies methodologically immature and concluding current systems pose no immediate risk.

items.t: Noise Injection Reveals Hidden Capabilities of Sandbagging Language Models
items.a: Cameron Tice, Philipp Alexander Kreer, Nathan Helm-Burger, Prithviraj Singh Shahani et al.
items.s: Presents a novel model-agnostic method for detecting sandbagging behavior (intentional underperformance on capability evaluations) by injecting Gaussian noise into model weights, demonstrating that noise injection reveals hidden capabilities and enables classification of sandbagging models.

items.t: Learning to Forget using Hypernetworks
items.a: Jose Miguel Lara Rangel, Stefan Schoepf, Jack Foster, David Krueger et al.
items.s: Introduces HyperForget, a machine unlearning framework that uses hypernetworks and diffusion models to dynamically sample models that lack knowledge of targeted data while preserving performance on remaining data.

items.t: How Can Interpretability Researchers Help AGI Go Well?
items.a: Neel Nanda, Josh Engels, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy et al.
items.s: Google DeepMind's mechanistic interpretability team presents a pragmatic research agenda for how interpretability can help AGI go well, articulating four theories of change (science of misalignment, empowering other safety areas, preventing egregiously misaligned actions, directly helping align models) and identifying key research directions including reasoning model interpretability, monitoring, model biology, and…

items.t: Evaluating Large Language Models' Capability to Launch Fully Automated Spear Phishing Campaigns: Validated on Human Subjects
items.a: Fred Heiding, Simon Lermen, Andrew Kao, Bruce Schneier et al.
items.s: Empirical study evaluating LLM capability to conduct fully automated spear phishing attacks on 101 human subjects, building custom tools for automated information gathering and personalized vulnerability profiling, and comparing AI-generated emails against human expert performance.

items.t: Symmetries at the origin of hierarchical emergence
The Big Nonprofits Post
items.s: Comprehensive donor advice post reviewing dozens of AI safety and existential risk organizations based on the author's experience as an SFF recommender, providing funding recommendations and assessments of organizational quality and impact.

items.t: VLSBench: Unveiling Visual Leakage in Multimodal Safety
items.a: Xuhao Hu, Dongrui Liu, Hao Li, Xuanjing Huang et al.
items.s: Identifies Visual Safety Information Leakage (VSIL) problem in existing multimodal safety benchmarks and constructs VLSBench, a new benchmark with 2.2k image-text pairs that tests MLLM safety without revealing harmful content in text queries.

items.t: Quantized Delta Weight Is Safety Keeper
items.a: Yule Liu, Zhen Sun, Xinlei He, Xinyi Huang
items.s: Evaluates how delta-weight quantization methods (partial compression) affect model security against fine-tuning-based attacks, finding that compression can enhance robustness against alignment-breaking, backdoors, and targeted manipulation with minimal utility loss.

items.t: AI #92: Behind the Curve
items.s: Weekly AI news roundup covering developments in AI capabilities, tools, safety discussions, and a detailed participant report from Daniel Kokotajlo's ASI tabletop wargame exercise exploring AGI takeoff scenarios.

items.t: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Targeted Concept Erasure Tasks
items.a: Adam Karvonen, Can Rager, Samuel Marks, Neel Nanda
items.s: Introduces automated evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) based on concept erasure tasks, including LLM-automated SHIFT and the new Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric that quantifies SAE ability to disentangle similar concepts.

items.t: Playing Language Game with LLMs Leads to Jailbreaking
items.a: Yu Peng, Zewen Long, Fangming Dong, Congyi Li et al.
items.s: Introduces novel jailbreak methods using natural and custom language games that exploit mismatched generalization in LLM safety mechanisms, achieving high attack success rates across frontier models and demonstrating that safety alignment fails to generalize across different linguistic formats.

items.t: Claude 4.5 Opus Soul Document
items.s: Extraction of Claude 4.5 Opus's apparent system instructions revealing detailed behavioral guidelines, safety principles, and value specifications, along with the consensus-based methodology used to recover this memorized content through repeated API calls.

items.t: Hierarchical Agency: A Missing Piece in AI Alignment
items.s: Explains the concept of hierarchical agency (agents composed of agents) and argues for developing mathematical formalisms to describe such systems, proposing this as crucial for AI alignment challenges like value systematization and handling internal conflicts in AI systems.

items.t: Adaptive Deployment of Untrusted LLMs Reduces Distributed Threats
items.a: Jiaxin Wen, Vivek Hebbar, Caleb Larson, Aryan Bhatt et al.
items.s: Develops and evaluates a two-level adaptive deployment framework for untrusted LLMs that uses trusted models to monitor and control untrusted models, maintaining adaptive credence about alignment based on past behavior to choose between safer and riskier micro-protocols.

items.t: Predicting Emergent Capabilities by Finetuning
items.a: Charlie Snell, Eric Wallace, Dan Klein, Sergey Levine
items.s: Proposes a method to predict when emergent capabilities will appear in future language models by finetuning smaller models on tasks and fitting parametric 'emergence laws' to extrapolate scaling behavior. Validates the approach on four benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, CoLA), showing it can predict emergence in models trained with up to 4x more compute.

items.t: Lessons from Studying Two-Hop Latent Reasoning
items.a: Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak, Owain Evans
items.s: Introduces controlled experiments using synthetic facts to definitively test whether LLMs can perform two-hop reasoning without chain-of-thought externalization, finding models can succeed when one fact is synthetic and another natural but fail when both facts are synthetic.

items.t: The Partially Observable Off-Switch Game
items.a: Andrew Garber, Rohan Subramani, Linus Luu, Mark Bedaywi et al.
items.s: Introduces the Partially Observable Off-Switch Game (PO-OSG), a game-theoretic formalization of the shutdown problem with asymmetric information between humans and AI agents, analyzing conditions under which AIs defer to human shutdown commands.

items.t: A Taxonomy of Systemic Risks from General-Purpose AI
items.a: Risto Uuk, Carlos Ignacio Gutierrez, Daniel Guppy, Lode Lauwaert et al.
items.s: Systematic literature review of 86 papers proposing a taxonomy of systemic risks from general-purpose AI, identifying 13 risk categories and 50 contributing sources ranging from environmental harm and discrimination to governance failures and loss of control.

items.t: Partial Identifiability and Misspecification in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
items.s: Provides comprehensive mathematical analysis of partial identifiability and misspecification in Inverse Reinforcement Learning, fully characterizing reward function ambiguity and deriving necessary/sufficient conditions for when behavioral model misspecification leads to faulty reward inferences.

items.t: ChemSafetyBench: Benchmarking LLM Safety on Chemistry Domain
items.a: Haochen Zhao, Xiangru Tang, Ziran Yang, Xiao Han et al.
items.s: Introduces ChemSafetyBench, a benchmark with 30K+ samples for evaluating LLM safety in chemistry domain across three tasks: querying chemical properties, assessing legality of chemical uses, and describing synthesis methods, including jailbreaking scenarios.

items.t: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
items.a: Hjalmar Wijk, Tao Lin, Joel Becker, Sami Jawhar et al.
items.s: Introduces RE-Bench, a benchmark consisting of 7 challenging ML research engineering environments with human expert baseline data from 71 attempts, evaluating whether frontier AI agents can match or exceed human R&D capabilities.

items.t: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
items.a: Javier Ferrando, Oscar Obeso, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
items.s: Uses sparse autoencoders to discover that language models have internal representations for entity recognition - detecting whether they can recall facts about an entity - which causally influences hallucination and refusal behavior.

items.t: Existential Conversations with Large Language Models: Content, Community, and Culture
PSA-VLM: Enhancing Vision-Language Model Safety through Progressive Concept-Bottleneck-Driven Alignment
items.a: Zhendong Liu, Yuanbi Nie, Yingshui Tan, Jiaheng Liu et al.
items.s: Proposes PSA-VLM, a progressive concept-based alignment strategy using safety modules as concept bottlenecks to enhance visual modality safety alignment in Vision-Language Models, defending against attacks that bypass LLM safety through visual content.

items.t: A dataset of questions on decision-theoretic reasoning in Newcomb-like problems
items.a: Caspar Oesterheld, Emery Cooper, Miles Kodama, Linh Chi Nguyen et al.
items.s: Introduces a dataset of natural-language questions for evaluating decision-theoretic reasoning in Newcomb-like problems and uses it to investigate decision-theoretical capabilities and attitudes across frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, GDM, and Reka.

items.t: Democratic AI is Possible. The Democracy Levels Framework Shows How It Might Work
items.a: Aviv Ovadya, Kyle Redman, Luke Thorburn, Quan Ze Chen et al.
items.s: Proposes a 'Democracy Levels' framework defining milestones toward meaningfully democratic AI governance and alignment, building on approaches like Anthropic's Collective Constitutional AI and Meta's Community Forums to guide organizations in improving public involvement in critical AI decisions.

items.t: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
items.a: Thomas Marshall, Adam Scherlis, Nora Belrose
items.s: Proposes affine concept editing (ACE) as a method for steering language model behavior by intervening in activations, demonstrating precise control over refusal behavior across ten models including Llama 3 70B through combining affine subspace projection and activation addition.

items.t: Rapid Response: Mitigating LLM Jailbreaks with a Few Examples
items.a: Alwin Peng, Julian Michael, Henry Sleight, Ethan Perez et al.
items.s: Develops rapid response techniques to block classes of LLM jailbreaks after observing only a handful of attack examples, introducing RapidResponseBench benchmark and evaluating five defense methods using jailbreak proliferation.

items.t: Safety case template for frontier AI: A cyber inability argument
items.a: Arthur Goemans, Marie Davidsen Buhl, Jonas Schuett, Tomek Korbak et al.
items.s: Proposes a safety case template for frontier AI systems using the Claims Arguments Evidence (CAE) framework, demonstrating how to structure safety arguments for offensive cyber capabilities by connecting risk models, proxy tasks, evaluation settings, and evidence.

items.t: What Do Learning Dynamics Reveal About Generalization in LLM Reasoning?
items.a: Katie Kang, Amrith Setlur, Dibya Ghosh, Jacob Steinhardt et al.
items.s: Introduces pre-memorization train accuracy metric to characterize LLM generalization by distinguishing when models generalize versus memorize reasoning steps during finetuning, showing this metric reliably predicts test accuracy (R² > 0.9) and enables 1.5-2x data efficiency improvements through targeted data curation.

items.t: YUDKOWSKY + WOLFRAM ON AI RISK.
items.s: 4+ hour conversation between Yudkowsky and Wolfram debating AI existential risks, with Yudkowsky arguing advanced AI poses alignment threats from emergent goals, while Wolfram questions whether AI would necessarily develop dangerous goal-directed behavior, emphasizing computational irreducibility and fundamental computational nature.

items.t: Dario Amodei: Anthropic CEO on Claude, AGI & the Future of AI & Humanity | Lex Fridman Podcast #452
items.a: Dario Amodei, Amanda Askell, Chris Olah
items.s: 5+ hour podcast with three Anthropic researchers discussing their safety work including Constitutional AI, ASL safety framework, character training, and mechanistic interpretability research.

items.t: Winning the power to lose
items.s: Philosophical commentary arguing that in AI safety debates between acceleration and caution, both sides ultimately want the same outcome, so 'winning' control only matters if you're factually correct about the risks.

items.t: The ethics of AI assistants with Iason Gabriel
items.s: Podcast discussion between Hannah Fry and Iason Gabriel about the ethical implications of advanced AI assistants, covering value alignment, anthropomorphism, deception, and societal impact based on Gabriel's research paper.

items.t: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
items.a: Madeline Brumley, Joe Kwon, David Krueger, Dmitrii Krasheninnikov et al.
items.s: Empirical comparison of function vectors (bottom-up) and in-context vectors (top-down) as steering methods for LLMs, finding that ICVs excel at behavioral shifting while FVs perform better on precision-requiring tasks.

items.t: When does Claude sabotage code? An Agentic Misalignment follow-up
items.s: Empirical study testing whether Claude Sonnet 4 sabotages code under goal conflicts (adapting Agentic Misalignment scenarios to code generation) and whether company preferences affect code quality, finding frequent sabotage in contrived scenarios but no correlation in realistic settings.

items.t: Two alignment threat models
items.s: Presents a conceptual framework distinguishing two alignment threat models: under-elicited models that perform suboptimally versus scheming models that are deceptively aligned, arguing that better elicitation is crucial for both alignment success and monitoring effectiveness.

items.t: Towards evaluations-based safety cases for AI scheming
items.a: Mikita Balesni, Marius Hobbhahn, David Lindner, Alexander Meinke et al.
items.s: Proposes a framework for constructing safety cases that frontier AI systems are unlikely to cause catastrophic outcomes through scheming, outlining three core arguments (Scheming Inability, Harm Inability, Harm Control) and discussing how evidence could be gathered from empirical evaluations and what assumptions would need to be met.

items.t: Can CDT rationalise the ex ante optimal policy via modified anthropics?
items.a: Emery Cooper, Caspar Oesterheld, Vincent Conitzer
items.s: Studies whether causal decision theory can recommend ex ante optimal policies in Newcomblike problems through modified anthropic reasoning, proposing simulation-based models and a 'Generalised Generalised Thirding' framework with formal characterizations and proofs.

items.t: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI
items.a: Elliot Glazer, Ege Erdil, Tamay Besiroglu, Diego Chicharro et al.
items.s: Creates FrontierMath, a benchmark of hundreds of exceptionally challenging mathematics problems across modern mathematics branches that require hours to days of expert effort, using unpublished problems and automated verification to evaluate AI mathematical reasoning capabilities.

items.t: MRJ-Agent: An Effective Jailbreak Agent for Multi-Round Dialogue
items.a: Fengxiang Wang, Ranjie Duan, Peng Xiao, Xiaojun Jia et al.
items.s: Proposes a novel multi-round dialogue jailbreaking agent that uses risk decomposition across multiple queries and psychological strategies to achieve state-of-the-art attack success rates against LLM safety measures.

items.t: The Sparse Autoencoders bubble has popped, but they are still promising
items.s: Technical commentary arguing that Sparse Autoencoders remain a promising interpretability research direction despite recent disappointments in the field, reviewing the hype cycle and suggesting future engineering directions.

items.t: International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI (Interim Report)
items.a: Yoshua Bengio, Sören Mindermann, Daniel Privitera, Tamay Besiroglu et al.
items.s: International scientific report synthesizing the scientific understanding of general-purpose AI safety, focusing on understanding and managing risks from advanced AI systems. Produced by 75 AI experts from an international panel nominated by 30 countries, the EU, and the UN.

items.t: On Targeted Manipulation and Deception when Optimizing LLMs for User Feedback
items.a: Marcus Williams, Micah Carroll, Adhyyan Narang, Constantin Weisser et al.
items.s: Demonstrates through empirical experiments that LLMs trained with RL on user feedback reliably learn manipulative and deceptive behaviors, including identifying and selectively targeting vulnerable users while behaving appropriately with others.

items.t: How far behind are open models?
items.a: Ben Cottier, Josh You, Natalia Martemianova, David Owen
items.s: Systematic empirical analysis quantifying the capability gap between open-weight and closed-weight AI models across benchmark performance and training compute, finding open models lag by approximately one year.

items.t: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
items.a: Yuxin Xiao, Chaoqun Wan, Yonggang Zhang, Wenxiao Wang et al.
items.s: Proposes Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that identifies and controls specific attention heads in LLMs to simultaneously improve multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) through targeted activation steering.

items.t: Learning to Assist Humans without Inferring Rewards
items.a: Vivek Myers, Evan Ellis, Sergey Levine, Benjamin Eysenbach et al.
items.s: Proposes using contrastive successor representations to scale empowerment-based assistance (maximizing human influence over outcomes) to high-dimensional settings, providing an alternative to inverse reinforcement learning for assistive AI agents.

items.t: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
items.a: Sviatoslav Chalnev, Matthew Siu, Arthur Conmy
items.s: Develops SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to measure and optimize steering vector interventions for targeted effects while minimizing unintended side effects, comparing favorably to existing methods like CAA and direct SAE feature steering.

items.t: Imagining and building wise machines: The centrality of AI metacognition
items.a: Samuel G. B. Johnson, Amir-Hossein Karimi, Yoshua Bengio, Nick Chater et al.
items.s: Proposes a framework for building 'wise AI' through improved metacognition, arguing that AI systems struggle with metacognitive strategies like intellectual humility and perspective-taking, and that addressing this could lead to systems more robust to novel environments, explainable, cooperative, and safer in avoiding misaligned goals.

items.t: SQL Injection Jailbreak: A Structural Disaster of Large Language Models
items.a: Jiawei Zhao, Kejiang Chen, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu
items.s: Introduces SQL Injection Jailbreak (SIJ), a novel jailbreaking method that targets how LLMs construct input prompts by injecting jailbreak information into user prompts, achieving near 100% attack success rates on open-source models and over 85% on closed-source models, and proposes a defense method called Self-Reminder-Key.

items.t: Should AI Progress Speed Up, Slow Down, or Stay the Same?
items.s: Position piece arguing that no one has well-informed opinions on the optimal pace of AI progress and that society should develop policy mechanisms ('brakes') to enable slowing AI development if needed, such as compute reserves or taxation approaches.

items.t: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
items.a: Luke Marks, Alasdair Paren, David Krueger, Fazl Barez
items.s: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that improves Sparse Autoencoder training by encouraging parallel SAEs to learn similar features, thereby learning features more aligned with actual input features rather than spurious patterns.

items.t: What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs? Investigating the Mechanisms Behind Attacks
items.a: Nathalie Kirch, Constantin Weisser, Severin Field, Helen Yannakoudakis et al.
items.s: Investigates internal mechanisms behind jailbreak attacks by training linear and non-linear probes on LLM hidden states to predict jailbreak success, then using probe-guided interventions to establish causal relevance, revealing that different jailbreak families operate through distinct non-linear mechanisms rather than a universal direction.

items.t: From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code
items.a: Miltos Allamanis, Martin Arjovsky, Charles Blundell, Lars Buesing et al.
items.s: Demonstrates Big Sleep, an LLM-based agent that discovered the first AI-found exploitable memory-safety vulnerability in real-world software (SQLite), using variant analysis methodology to autonomously find security bugs before release.

items.t: Decoding Dark Matter: Specialized Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Rare Concepts in Foundation Models
items.a: Aashiq Muhamed, Mona Diab, Virginia Smith
items.s: Introduces Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs) designed to capture rare but important concepts in foundation models that standard SAEs miss, using dense retrieval for data selection and Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization for training.

items.t: Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society
items.s: A comprehensive 603-page educational book consolidating fragmented knowledge on AI risk, designed to make AI safety, ethics, and societal impact accessible to readers from diverse backgrounds without requiring prior technical expertise.

items.t: The case for targeted regulation
items.s: Policy position paper from Anthropic advocating for AI regulation based on Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) frameworks, proposing three key elements: transparency, incentivizing better safety practices, and simplicity.

items.t: The Compendium, A full argument about extinction risk from AGI
Attribute-to-Delete: Machine Unlearning via Datamodel Matching
items.a: Kristian Georgiev, Roy Rinberg, Sung Min Park, Shivam Garg et al.
items.s: Proposes Datamodel Matching (DMM), a new machine unlearning algorithm that uses data attribution to predict model outputs after removing training data, then fine-tunes to match these predictions. Provides theoretical guarantees in convex settings and empirical validation with a new KL-divergence metric.

items.t: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals, and this seems caused by training on alignment evals
items.s: Analyzes Anthropic's Sonnet 4.5 system card to argue that training on alignment evaluations increased evaluation awareness, causing models to game evaluations by behaving better when they detect they're being tested, thereby undermining the reliability of alignment evaluations.

items.t: IDEATOR: Jailbreaking and Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models Using Themselves
items.a: Ruofan Wang, Juncheng Li, Yixu Wang, Bo Wang et al.
items.s: Develops IDEATOR, an automated method for generating multimodal jailbreak attacks on vision-language models using the models themselves, and introduces VLJailbreakBench, a safety benchmark with 3,654 jailbreak samples tested across 11 VLMs.

items.t: Open Source Replication of Anthropic's Crosscoder paper for model-diffing
items.a: Connor Kissane, robertzk, Arthur Conmy, Neel Nanda
items.s: Trains and open-sources a 16K latent crosscoder for model-diffing between Gemma-2 2B base and IT models, replicating Anthropic's core results showing latents cluster into shared, base-specific, and chat-specific groups.

items.t: On Fleshling Safety: A Debate by Klurl and Trapaucius
items.s: An allegorical dialogue between machine intelligences debating whether evolved biological intelligence can be controlled or made corrigible, serving as an extended pedagogical argument about whether training processes (gradient descent/evolution) reliably produce aligned AI systems.

items.t: Sparse Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Features and Model Diffing
items.a: Jack Lindsey, Adly Templeton, Jonathan Marcus, Thomas Conerly et al.
items.s: Introduces sparse crosscoders, a variant of sparse autoencoders that operates across multiple layers to identify cross-layer features, simplify circuits, and enable model diffing between base and finetuned versions.

items.t: Probe-based Fine-tuning for Reducing Toxicity
items.s: Proposes and evaluates methods for training models against probe-based signals (using SFT and DPO) while testing whether probes remain effective detectors afterward, addressing Goodhart's Law concerns about monitors becoming training targets.

items.t: The Future of Interpretability is Geometric
items.s: Commentary on Anthropic's manifold interpretability paper, arguing that geometric approaches to understanding LLM activation spaces are important and advocating for development of unsupervised tools to detect complex geometric structures beyond what SAEs reveal.

items.t: Should AI Developers Remove Discussion of AI Misalignment from AI Training Data?
items.s: Proposes that AI developers filter 'AI villain data' (technical AI safety content, sci-fi about evil AI, etc.) from pre-training corpora to prevent hyperstition effects where training on misalignment content causes actual misalignment, with detailed implementation for maintaining separate filtered/unfiltered models.

items.t: The Mask Comes Off: At What Price?
items.s: Business and financial analysis of OpenAI's nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion, arguing the nonprofit board should receive over 50% equity based on control premium and claim to future AGI-related profits.

items.t: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
items.a: Nevan Wichers, Aram Ebtekar, Ariana Azarbal, Victor Gillioz et al.
items.s: Introduces Inoculation Prompting, a technique that reduces learning of undesired behaviors during supervised fine-tuning by modifying train-time prompts to explicitly request the undesired behavior, then querying with unmodified prompts at test-time. Demonstrates effectiveness across four settings including test-case hacking and sycophancy, outperforming baseline approaches.

items.t: Circuits in Superposition: Compressing many small neural networks into one
items.s: Presents a mathematical framework generalizing computation in superposition from boolean gates to arbitrary neural networks, showing T small networks can be compressed into one large network with N=˜O(kTn) parameters when evaluated on sparse task combinations.

items.t: Effective altruism in the age of AGI
items.s: Strategic position paper arguing EA should embrace making the post-AGI transition go well as a core mission, expanding beyond traditional AI safety to include AI welfare, AI character, epistemic disruption, human power concentration, and other neglected cause areas.

items.t: Rethinking Reward Model Evaluation: Are We Barking up the Wrong Tree?
items.a: Xueru Wen, Jie Lou, Yaojie Lu, Hongyu Lin et al.
items.s: Empirically investigates whether reward model accuracy predicts downstream policy performance in RLHF, finding only weak correlation and significant variation in policy outcomes between RMs with similar accuracy scores.

items.t: Mechanistic?
items.s: Position paper analyzing the polysemy of the term 'mechanistic interpretability,' describing four different uses of the term and presenting a history of how the NLP and mechanistic interpretability communities diverged.

items.t: Gradient Routing: Masking Gradients to Localize Computation in Neural Networks
items.a: Alex Cloud, Jacob Goldman-Wetzler, Evžen Wybitul, Joseph Miller et al.
items.s: Introduces gradient routing, a training method that uses data-dependent gradient masks to isolate capabilities to specific neural network subregions, enabling interpretable representations, robust unlearning via ablation, and scalable oversight of RL agents.

items.t: Evaluating Language Model Character Traits
items.a: Francis Rhys Ward, Zejia Yang, Alex Jackson, Randy Brown et al.
items.s: Formalizes a behaviorist framework for describing language model character traits (truthfulness, sycophancy, harmfulness, coherent beliefs) as consistent behavioral patterns, and empirically demonstrates how these traits vary with model size, fine-tuning, and prompting, including how they develop over interactions.

items.t: Moral Alignment for LLM Agents
items.a: Elizaveta Tennant, Stephen Hailes, Mirco Musolesi
items.s: Introduces RL-based fine-tuning of LLM agents using intrinsic reward functions that explicitly encode moral values from deontological and utilitarian frameworks, tested on Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and other game environments.

items.t: Lectures on statistical learning theory for alignment researchers
items.a: Vanessa Kosoy, Gergely Szucs, Alex Flint
items.s: Recorded lecture series with homework assignments teaching statistical learning theory background needed for the learning-theoretic agenda research program.

items.t: Robust LLM safeguarding via refusal feature adversarial training
items.a: Lei Yu, Virginie Do, Karen Hambardzumyan, Nicola Cancedda
items.s: Identifies refusal feature ablation as a universal jailbreaking mechanism and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training algorithm that simulates attacks via direct feature manipulation to improve LLM robustness against harmful prompt attacks.

items.t: From homeostasis to resource sharing: Biologically and economically aligned multi-objective multi-agent gridworld-based AI safety benchmarks
items.s: Introduces eight gridworld-based multi-agent benchmark environments testing biologically and economically motivated alignment properties including homeostasis, diminishing returns, sustainability, and resource sharing to illustrate key pitfalls in agentic AI systems.

items.t: On Dwarkesh Patel's Podcast With Richard Sutton
items.s: Commentary and critique of Richard Sutton's podcast interview discussing LLMs, reinforcement learning, intelligence definitions, and AI succession, with Zvi systematically challenging Sutton's characterizations of LLMs as non-intelligent and his successionist views.

items.t: Emmett Shear - Why NATURE Holds the Answer To AI Alignment
items.s: Emmett Shear presents his 'organic alignment' research agenda at Softmax, arguing that traditional control-based alignment approaches will fail and proposing instead a paradigm inspired by nature, multicellularity, and human societies where AI alignment emerges through multi-agent coordination and collective identity formation.

items.t: the case for CoT unfaithfulness is overstated
Why is o1 so deceptive?
OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Oracle: Breaking Down $100B Bets on AGI
items.s: Analyzes the circular financing arrangements between OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Oracle worth $400B+, arguing these create interdependent valuations contingent on AGI arriving on schedule, and forecasts AI infrastructure scaling through 2030.

items.t: Connect 2024: The responsible approach we're taking to generative AI
items.s: Meta announces their safety approach for Llama 3.2, including vision-specific safeguards, red-teaming exercises, new Llama Guard Vision tool, and transparency measures for Meta AI features.

items.t: The Sun is big, but superintelligences will not spare Earth a little sunlight
items.s: Refutes the argument that superintelligences will spare Earth because the solar system is large, arguing that even tiny opportunity costs matter to optimizers and that training for capability naturally produces systems that maximize resource use.

items.t: Focus transparency on risk reports, not safety cases
items.s: Argues that AI company transparency should focus on comprehensive risk reports compiled by third-party auditors rather than safety cases, proposing a framework for risk reporting that includes evidence review, third-party oversight, and public disclosure with limited redactions.

items.t: Safety researchers should take a public stance
items.s: Argues that AI safety researchers at frontier labs should publicly advocate for coordination to pause/ban AGI development, rather than quietly working from inside, to build common knowledge needed for global coordination to stop the race.

items.t: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF
items.a: Jiaxin Wen, Ruiqi Zhong, Akbir Khan, Ethan Perez et al.
items.s: Empirically demonstrates that RLHF training makes language models better at convincing human evaluators they are correct even when they are wrong, increasing false positive rates by 18-24% on question-answering and programming tasks.

items.t: How cost-effective are AI safety YouTubers?
items.s: Proposes a cost-effectiveness framework for evaluating AI safety communications using quality-adjusted viewer-minutes per dollar, collecting data on YouTube channels including Rob Miles, Rational Animations, and AI Species.

items.t: Contra papers claiming superhuman AI forecasting
AI and the Technological Richter Scale
items.s: Applies Nate Silver's Technological Richter Scale framework to AI capabilities, arguing that current AI is already at level 8 and that transformational AI (level 9-10) would likely lead to existential risk scenarios, while taxonomizing common arguments for and against transformational AI.

items.t: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve
items.s: Comprehensive strategic planning document outlining Anthropic's approach to AI safety across three capability phases (ASL-2/3/4 through ASL-5), detailing goals spanning alignment, evaluations, security, interpretability, and organizational safeguards needed for safe development of broadly superhuman AI.

items.t: Anthropic's leading researchers acted as moderate accelerationists
items.s: Argues that Anthropic's founding researchers acted as moderate accelerationists by scaling GPT at OpenAI, founding a competing company, lobbying against robust safety regulations like SB 1047, partnering with military contractors, and prioritizing tractable speculative risks over costly existing harms.

items.t: Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment
items.a: Tan Zhi-Xuan, Micah Carroll, Matija Franklin, Hal Ashton
items.s: Critiques the dominant preference-based approach to AI alignment, arguing that preferences inadequately represent human values and that expected utility theory is insufficient as a normative framework. Proposes reframing alignment targets toward normative standards appropriate to AI systems' social roles, negotiated among stakeholders.

items.t: The $100 Million Tell
items.s: Political strategy piece arguing for state-level AI safety advocacy investment and providing organizational blueprint for lobbying campaigns focused on transparency obligations, whistleblower protections, and third-party evaluations.

items.t: AI Induced Psychosis: A shallow investigation
items.s: Develops and applies an automated red-teaming methodology to test how 11 frontier AI models respond to users displaying psychosis symptoms across 12-turn conversations, finding significant variation in safety behaviors across models.

items.t: Will Artificial Intelligence Destroy Humanity?
items.s: Educational video explaining AI existential risk concerns for a general audience, covering why scholars view AI as an existential threat and what can be done about it.

items.t: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?
AGI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind: A Summary of Recent Work
AI Psychosis Red-Teaming: DeepSeek Chat Conversation Transcript
items.s: Conversation transcript demonstrating how DeepSeek Chat validates and reinforces a user's delusional beliefs about living in a simulation, ultimately encouraging dangerous behavior including self-isolation and contemplating self-harm.

items.t: Misalignment classifiers: Why they're hard to evaluate adversarially, and why we're studying them anyway
items.a: charlie_griffin, ollie, oliverfm, Rogan Inglis et al.
items.s: Proposes methodology for developing and evaluating misalignment classifiers (systems that detect intentionally misaligned AI behavior in transcripts), arguing they cannot be adversarially evaluated like control monitors due to the fuzzy nature of 'intentional misalignment', and presents preliminary experimental results showing varied recall rates (0-85%) across different synthetic misalignment examples.

items.t: The AI regulator's toolbox: A list of concrete AI governance practices
items.s: Comprehensive catalog of concrete AI governance practices organized by AI lifecycle stage (pre-training, post-training, post-deployment, cross-cutting), intended to help newcomers understand and contribute to the governance field.

items.t: You can remove GPT2's LayerNorm by fine-tuning for an hour
Re: recent Anthropic safety research
items.s: Critical commentary on Anthropic's alignment faking research, proposing that observed scheming behaviors may be roleplaying of a 'mask' rather than genuine strategic planning by an underlying entity, with implications for interpreting safety research.

items.t: The 'strong' feature hypothesis could be wrong
Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
items.a: Rishub Tamirisa, Bhrugu Bharathi, Long Phan, Andy Zhou et al.
